Real Solver Interface and First Dry-Run Architecture for the A=22A=22 Renormalized F0/F2F0/F2 Nuclear Matrix-Element Pipeline
Connecting the Farid Nuclear Framework to a Real Many-Body Engine
________________________________________
Abstract
The software shell for the A=22A=22 renormalized F0/F2F0/F2 nuclear matrix-element production pipeline has been established. The decisive next step is to identify which real nuclear many-body solver should generate the first physical wavefunctions and matrix elements. This article addresses that question by defining a two-lane computational strategy: a shell-model integration route (Lane S) using KSHELL or a comparable configuration-interaction code for real wavefunction generation and independent diagonalization checks, and a valence-space IMSRG production route (Lane I) using imsrg++ or an equivalent code for consistent Hamiltonian and custom-operator evolution under a unitary transformation. The central requirement is that a real eigenvector alone is insufficient; a physical Farid matrix element additionally requires a correctly constructed two-body operator, consistent operator evolution, and independent validation. We define the custom two-body matrix-element (TBME) interface, the Feynman–Hellmann validation protocol, the dry-run sequence (D0–D3), and the mandatory certificates required before any physical M0,22RM0,22R or R2,22RR2,22R may be claimed. At present, the solver architecture is selected but all physical fields remain NOT COMPUTED until an actual nuclear many-body engine is executed.
________________________________________
1. Introduction: The Need for a Real Solver
The software architecture established in the preceding specification provides the validation shell for the first physical Farid nuclear matrix-element calculation. What remains is a practical question of central importance:
Which real nuclear solver should generate the first A=22 wavefunctions and F0/F2 matrix elements?Which real nuclear solver should generate the first A=22 wavefunctions and F0/F2 matrix elements?
The answer must simultaneously satisfy two requirements:
realistic many-body nuclear structurerealistic many-body nuclear structure
and:
consistent treatment of our custom two-body operators.consistent treatment of our custom two-body operators.
The second requirement is decisive. A solver that produces realistic nuclear energies but cannot accept arbitrary two-body operators is insufficient for this programme.
________________________________________
2. Solver Strategy: A Two-Lane Architecture
The recommended approach uses two complementary computational lanes:
Lane S — shell-model integration and dry-run validationLane S — shell-model integration and dry-run validation
followed by:
Lane I — VS-IMSRG production with evolved-operator consistencyLane I — VS-IMSRG production with evolved-operator consistency
Lane S tests the real wavefunction and diagonalization infrastructure. Lane I provides the more rigorous route for consistent Hamiltonian and custom-operator evolution.
________________________________________
3. Why Both Lanes Are Necessary
KSHELL is a genuine large-scale configuration-interaction shell-model code. Public versions can generate shell-model states and wavefunctions from .snt interaction files and .ptn partition files, and support large-scale diagonalization.
The imsrg++ software, independently, is publicly available and capable of Hartree–Fock, single-reference IM-SRG, and valence-space IMSRG calculations, with C++ implementation and Python bindings.
These capabilities are complementary. KSHELL provides real shell-model wavefunctions for interface validation. The IMSRG route provides consistent operator evolution for the physically renormalized result.
________________________________________
4. The Custom-Operator Wall
The required quantities are not standard electromagnetic observables. They are:
O0=∑i<jf0(rij) τi⋅τjO0=i<j∑f0(rij)τi⋅τj
and:
O2=∑i<jf2(rij)[3τ3iτ3j−τi⋅τj]O2=i<j∑f2(rij)[3τ3iτ3j−τi⋅τj]
A solver that merely calculates standard electromagnetic transitions is not sufficient. The production engine must accept or generate arbitrary two-body operator matrix elements.
Conclusion:
Stock KSHELL alone≠complete Farid production engineStock KSHELL alone=complete Farid production engine
The custom F0/F2F0/F2 operator requires an additional matrix-element and TBME interface that must be built explicitly.
________________________________________
5. Recommended Production Architecture
The preferred eventual production chain is:
microscopic nuclear interactionmicroscopic nuclear interaction⇓⇓VS-IMSRG transformationVS-IMSRG transformation⇓⇓HeffHeff
and simultaneously:
O0,eff,O2,effO0,eff,O2,eff⇓⇓valence-space diagonalizationvalence-space diagonalization⇓⇓⟨O0,eff⟩,⟨O2,eff⟩⟨O0,eff⟩,⟨O2,eff⟩
________________________________________
6. Why imsrg++ Is Strategically Useful
The imsrg++ software explicitly supports valence-space IMSRG calculations and has machinery for evolved operators. Its public repository documents additional machinery for three-body normal-ordering and tensor IMSRG developments.
It is therefore closer to the theoretical requirement:
Okeff=UOkU†Okeff=UOkU†
than a diagonalizer alone.
However, imsrg++ does not automatically contain F0/F2F0/F2. The Farid operators are new operators defined in this programme. They must be implemented explicitly as two-body matrix elements in the single-particle basis. The software cannot simply be asked for "F2" by name. The required chain is:
fk(r)+isospin tensorfk(r)+isospin tensor⇓⇓two-body basis matrix elementstwo-body basis matrix elements⇓⇓IMSRG Operator objectIMSRG Operator object⇓⇓evolved Okeffevolved Okeff
________________________________________

The first dry run should not attempt to claim a physical M0RM0R or M2RM2R. Instead it should establish that the pipeline can successfully execute:
22Mg,22Na,22Ne22Mg,22Na,22Ne
through a real shell-model solver and recover the target 0+0+ states.
The first certificate is therefore:
A22_REAL_SOLVER_CONNECTEDA22_REAL_SOLVER_CONNECTED
This means a real solver executed, real shell-model Hamiltonian loaded, wavefunctions generated, target states identified, and output parser working. It does not mean F0/F2F0/F2 matrix elements have been physically computed.

10. Custom Two-Body Matrix-Element Interface
Once real wavefunctions are available, the next requirement is:
⟨Ψ∣Ok∣Ψ⟩⟨Ψ∣Ok∣Ψ⟩
This demands either a solver capable of contracting arbitrary two-body operator TBMEs with shell-model two-body densities, or a modification of the transition-density machinery.
10.1 Preferred Mathematical Contraction
For a two-body operator:
⟨Ψ∣Ok∣Ψ⟩=∑abcdJTρabcdJT(2) OabcdJT(k)⟨Ψ∣Ok∣Ψ⟩=abcdJT∑ρabcdJT(2)OabcdJT(k)
Here ρ(2)ρ(2) is the two-body density matrix and O(k)O(k) contains the F0/F2F0/F2 two-body matrix elements.
This is the correct generic bridge from shell-model wavefunctions to arbitrary two-body observables. Once ρ(2)ρ(2) is available, the nuclear wavefunction calculation and the Farid operator calculation remain cleanly separated:
wavefunction→ρ(2)wavefunction→ρ(2)
and:
fk(r)→OabcdJT(k)fk(r)→OabcdJT(k)
Then they meet only at the contraction.

11. TBME Generator
A dedicated module should be created:

11.1 Required TBME Form
For two-particle basis states ∣(ab)JT⟩∣(ab)JT⟩, calculate:
⟨(ab)JT∣f0(r12)τ1⋅τ2∣(cd)JT⟩⟨(ab)JT∣f0(r12)τ1⋅τ2∣(cd)JT⟩
and:

11.2 Isospin Channel Unit Test for F0F0
For two nucleons:
τ1⋅τ2=2T12(T12+1)−3τ1⋅τ2=2T12(T12+1)−3
Therefore:
•	T12=1⇒+1T12=1⇒+1
•	T12=0⇒−3T12=0⇒−3
The TBME generator must reproduce this exactly before radial physics is included.
11.3 F2F2 Tensor Test
The isotensor operator must obey the correct rank-two structure. Its triplet-level output must ultimately reproduce:
1:−2:11:−2:1
Any TBME generator that fails the coherent tensor tests is rejected before a many-body run.

12. Radial Basis and Oscillator Dependence
For an oscillator-basis shell-model implementation, the radial integrals take schematic form:
Iabcd(k)=⟨ab∣fk(r12)∣cd⟩Iabcd(k)=⟨ab∣fk(r12)∣cd⟩
These require transformation to relative and center-of-mass coordinates or an equivalent established two-body basis procedure. No crude average-radius substitution is acceptable for production.
If harmonic-oscillator single-particle states are used, the TBMEs depend on the oscillator parameter ℏωℏω or oscillator length bb. This parameter belongs in the nuclear calculation manifest and uncertainty study. It must not be tuned to increase or decrease F2F2.

17. Feynman–Hellmann Validation in the Real Solver
After obtaining the direct finite-range result, perturb:

17.1 Do Not Confuse Bare and Effective Hamiltonians
If a valence-space effective calculation is used, the FH procedure must be defined consistently. One cannot necessarily add a bare operator after the IMSRG decoupling and call the result identical to perturbing the initial microscopic Hamiltonian.
17.2 Preferred Rigorous FH Test
At high rigor, perform two conceptually equivalent calculations. Route A: evolve HH and OkOk consistently and evaluate the matrix element. Route B: introduce a small source term H(ϵ)=H+ϵOkH(ϵ)=H+ϵOk upstream and repeat the decoupling. Then compare dEdϵdϵdE with the evolved-operator expectation.
Route B is more expensive because the many-body transformation may need to be repeated for multiple ϵϵ values. It is therefore primarily a validation calculation, not the routine method for every production point.

To guarantee absolute traceability, every certificate generated by the validation suite is bound to an immutable run manifest. The manifest records:

Construction of the F0/F2F0/F2 Two-Body Matrix Elements: From Coordinate-Space Operators to Solver-Ready Antisymmetrized Harmonic-Oscillator TBMEs
A Rigorous Mathematical and Computational Framework for the Farid Nuclear Operator Interface
\
Abstract
The Farid F0/F2F0/F2 nuclear operators are defined in coordinate space as two-body isospin-dependent interactions. A shell-model or IMSRG solver, however, does not operate directly on symbolic coordinate-space expressions; it requires antisymmetrized two-body matrix elements (TBMEs) in a coupled harmonic-oscillator basis. This article constructs the exact bridge between these two representations. We define three distinct spaces — single-particle coordinates, relative and center-of-mass coordinates, and the antisymmetrized shell-model TBME basis — and derive the transformation chain connecting them: radial harmonic-oscillator integrals, Talmi–Moshinsky transformation, angular and isospin recoupling, and fermionic antisymmetrization. A critical technical point is established: F0F0 is an isospin scalar and admits a standard scalar JTJT-coupled TBME representation, but F2F2 is a rank-2 isospin tensor whose T3T3-dependent structure — pp:+2pp:+2, pn(T=1):−4pn(T=1):−4, nn:+2nn:+2, T=0:0T=0:0 — cannot be represented by a scalar JTJT TBME table alone. We derive the exact pair-level algebra for both operators, establish the Pauli antisymmetry conditions, define the transformation to jjjj-coupled single-particle basis via Talmi–Moshinsky brackets, and specify a comprehensive validation suite (U1–U12) that must pass before any TBME file is admitted into a nuclear solver. Two further corrections are established: (i) the unit-normalized finite-range kernel does not reduce to the coherent operator f=1f=1 as Rnuc→∞Rnuc→∞, and (ii) any "damping ratio" M(R)/PM(R)/P must be dimensionally audited, because the finite-range matrix element carries dimension L−3L−3 whereas the coherent algebraic benchmark is dimensionless.
________________________________________
1. Introduction: The Need for a Solver-Ready Operator
The Farid F0/F2F0/F2 nuclear operators are presently defined in coordinate space:
O0=∑i<jf0(rij) τi⋅τjO0=i<j∑f0(rij)τi⋅τj
and:
O2=∑i<jf2(rij)[3τ3iτ3j−τi⋅τj]O2=i<j∑f2(rij)[3τ3iτ3j−τi⋅τj]
A shell-model or IMSRG solver does not operate directly on this symbolic expression. It requires two-body matrix elements:
⟨ab;J∣Ok∣cd;J⟩⟨ab;J∣Ok∣cd;J⟩
or an equivalent coupled representation. The construction of TBMEs of central interactions in an oscillator basis can be reduced, through Talmi–Moshinsky techniques, to radial Talmi integrals combined with transformation coefficients.
This article constructs the exact bridge:
coordinate-space Ok→relative HO matrix elements→Moshinsky transformation→antisymmetrized TBMEs→solver inputcoordinate-space Ok→relative HO matrix elements→Moshinsky transformation→antisymmetrized TBMEs→solver input
________________________________________
2. Three Spaces Must Be Distinguished
The calculation involves three different representations.
Space A — single-particle coordinates:
∣α1α2⟩=∣n1l1j1m1, n2l2j2m2⟩∣α1α2⟩=∣n1l1j1m1,n2l2j2m2⟩
Space B — relative and center-of-mass coordinates:
∣nl,NL;⋯ ⟩∣nl,NL;⋯⟩
Space C — antisymmetrized shell-model TBME basis:
∣(ab)JM;TT3⟩A∣(ab)JM;TT3⟩A
or the proton-neutron analogue. The operator is simplest in Space B, while the many-body solver generally requires Space C.
________________________________________
3. Relative Coordinate Convention
Choose the dimensionless orthogonal Jacobi convention:
ρ=r1−r22ρ=2r1−r2R=r1+r22R=2r1+r2
Then:
r12=∣r1−r2∣=2 ρr12=∣r1−r2∣=2ρ
This convention must be frozen because missing the factor 22 changes every finite-range radial matrix element.
Alternatively, one may use the physical relative coordinate:
r=r1−r2,Rcm=r1+r22r=r1−r2,Rcm=2r1+r2
Both are valid, but the oscillator length associated with the relative coordinate changes. Therefore the coordinate convention and the oscillator-length convention must always be stored together.
________________________________________
4. Harmonic-Oscillator Single-Particle Basis
A single-particle state is:
∣a⟩=∣nalajama,ta⟩∣a⟩=∣nalajama,ta⟩
The spatial radial function is:
Rnl(r;b)=Nnl(rb)le−r2/(2b2)Lnl+1/2(r2b2)Rnl(r;b)=Nnl(br)le−r2/(2b2)Lnl+1/2(b2r2)
with normalization:
∫0∞r2∣Rnl(r;b)∣2dr=1∫0∞r2∣Rnl(r;b)∣2dr=1
The oscillator length is:
b=ℏmNωb=mNωℏ
with associated parameter ℏωℏω. The chosen bb or ℏωℏω must come from the declared nuclear-model setup. It is not a Farid coupling parameter.
________________________________________
5. Translational Invariance and Moshinsky Transformation
Because fk=fk(r12)fk=fk(r12), the Farid pair operators depend only on relative coordinates. Thus they are intrinsically translationally invariant at the two-body level. The Moshinsky transformation isolates the relative coordinate from center-of-mass motion.
Two single-particle oscillator states may be transformed according to:
∣n1l1,n2l2;ΛMΛ⟩=∑nlNL⟨nl,NL;Λ∣n1l1,n2l2;Λ⟩∣nl,NL;ΛMΛ⟩∣n1l1,n2l2;ΛMΛ⟩=nlNL∑⟨nl,NL;Λ∣n1l1,n2l2;Λ⟩∣nl,NL;ΛMΛ⟩
The coefficient:
⟨nl,NL;Λ∣n1l1,n2l2;Λ⟩⟨nl,NL;Λ∣n1l1,n2l2;Λ⟩
is a Talmi–Moshinsky bracket. The transformation obeys oscillator-quanta conservation:
2n1+l1+2n2+l2=2n+l+2N+L2n1+l1+2n2+l2=2n+l+2N+L
Any Moshinsky implementation violating this identity must fail immediately.
________________________________________
6. Central Radial Integral
Because our radial kernels depend only on r12r12, in relative coordinates:
⟨nl,NL∣f(r12)∣n′l′,N′L′⟩⟨nl,NL∣f(r12)∣n′l′,N′L′⟩
is diagonal in the center-of-mass quantum numbers:
N=N′,L=L′N=N′,L=L′
For a central radial kernel it is also diagonal in relative orbital angular momentum:
l=l′l=l′
Define the fundamental radial object:
Inn′l(k)=∫0∞dρ ρ2 Rnl(ρ;b) fk(2ρ) Rn′l(ρ;b)Inn′l(k)=∫0∞dρρ2Rnl(ρ;b)fk(2ρ)Rn′l(ρ;b)
The 22 follows from the locked Jacobi convention.
Dimensional ledger: If [fk]=L−3[fk]=L−3, then:
[Inn′l(k)]=L−3[Inn′l(k)]=L−3
The isospin factors are dimensionless. Hence the raw finite-range TBMEs also carry dimension L−3L−3 under this normalization.
________________________________________
7. Kernel Definitions
Gaussian regulated kernel:
fC(r;R)=1π3/2R3e−r2/R2fC(r;R)=π3/2R31e−r2/R2
with ∫d3r fC(r;R)=1∫d3rfC(r;R)=1. In the Jacobi coordinate:
fC(2ρ;R)=1π3/2R3e−2ρ2/R2fC(2ρ;R)=π3/2R31e−2ρ2/R2
Internal Yukawa kernel:
fY(r;R)=e−r/R4πR2rfY(r;R)=4πR2re−r/R
with ∫d3r fY(r;R)=1∫d3rfY(r;R)=1. In Jacobi coordinates:
fY(2ρ;R)=e−2ρ/R4πR22ρfY(2ρ;R)=4πR22ρe−2ρ/R
________________________________________
8. Numerical Radial Evaluation
For arbitrary n,n′,ln,n′,l, the radial integral may be evaluated using high-order quadrature. The implementation should provide both an analytic special-case route and a general numerical quadrature route.
Dimensionless integration variable: Set x=ρ/bx=ρ/b. Then:
Inn′l(k)=∫0∞dx x2 R~nl(x) b3fk(2bx) R~n′l(x) b−3Inn′l(k)=∫0∞dxx2Rnl(x)b3fk(2bx)Rn′l(x)b−3
This makes the dependence on R/bR/b explicit.
Ground-relative-state analytic test: For n=n′=0n=n′=0, l=0l=0, the relative HO probability density is Gaussian. The Gaussian-contact expectation has an analytic closed form:
IC(b,R)=1π3/2(b2+R2)3/2IC(b,R)=π3/2(b2+R2)3/21
However, the production physical kernel is defined as a function of r12=2ρr12=2ρ. Therefore the analytic expression used for a production unit test must incorporate the corresponding rescaling of RR.
________________________________________
9. The F0F0 Pair Algebra
For two nucleons with pair isospin T12T12:
τ1⋅τ2=2T12(T12+1)−3τ1⋅τ2=2T12(T12+1)−3
Therefore:
T12=1⇒+1T12=1⇒+1T12=0⇒−3T12=0⇒−3
This is exact. In a good-TT relative basis:
⟨nlST∣O0∣n′lST⟩=Inn′l(0)[2T(T+1)−3]⟨nlST∣O0∣n′lST⟩=Inn′l(0)[2T(T+1)−3]
No pair-TT mixing occurs because O0O0 is an isoscalar.
________________________________________
10. The F2F2 Isotensor Algebra: A Critical Correction
Define:
Θ2=3τ31τ32−τ1⋅τ2Θ2=3τ31τ32−τ1⋅τ2
This is the q=0q=0 component, up to convention-dependent normalization, of an isospin rank-two operator. It is not an isospin scalar.
Therefore a TBME implementation that stores only one number for a given pair TT, independent of T3T3, cannot fully represent F2F2.
Exact two-nucleon F2F2 values:
Using τ3(p)=+1τ3(p)=+1, τ3(n)=−1τ3(n)=−1:
Pair	(T,T3)(T,T3)
Θ2Θ2

pppp	(1,+1)(1,+1)	+2+2
pn+nppn+np	(1,0)(1,0)	−4−4
nnnn	(1,−1)(1,−1)	+2+2
pn−nppn−np	(0,0)(0,0)	00
This table becomes a hard TBME unit test.
Why F2F2 vanishes in pair T=0T=0: The Wigner–Eckart triangle condition for an isospin tensor of rank K=2K=2 is:
∣T−T′∣≤K≤T+T′∣T−T′∣≤K≤T+T′
For T=T′=0T=T′=0, rank 2 cannot act diagonally.
________________________________________
11. Reduced-Tensor Representation
In a fully isospin-coupled code one should represent O2O2 through reduced matrix elements:
⟨T′∥O(2)∥T⟩⟨T′∥O(2)∥T⟩
and recover the T3T3-dependent matrix element using a Clebsch–Gordan or 3j3j coefficient. The exact proportionality convention must be locked with the code.
For KSHELL-like proton-neutron TBME storage, an easier route may be explicit charge-channel TBMEs:
O2pp=+2I,O2nn=+2IO2pp=+2I,O2nn=+2I
and in the properly symmetrized T=1T=1 pn sector:
O2pn,T=1=−4IO2pn,T=1=−4I
The T=0T=0 pn sector is zero. This representation must still respect antisymmetrization.
Critical implementation rule: Do not simply multiply every proton-neutron product-state TBME by −4−4. A raw ordered state ∣pn⟩∣pn⟩ is not identical to the good-isospin T=1T=1 combination. The pn exchange structure must be treated consistently with the solver's basis convention.
________________________________________
12. Antisymmetry Requirements
For identical nucleons, a relative two-body state must satisfy fermionic antisymmetry. For good L,S,TL,S,T, the condition is:
(−1)l+S+T=−1(−1)l+S+T=−1
Equivalently:
l+S+Tmust be oddl+S+Tmust be odd
Examples: For an SS-wave (l=0l=0):
•	Spin singlet S=0S=0 requires T=1T=1, giving 1S01S0.
•	Spin triplet S=1S=1 requires T=0T=0, giving 3S13S1.
Immediate implication for F2F2: Since F2F2 vanishes in pair T=0T=0, the leading SS-wave F2F2 response resides in the 1S01S0, T=1T=1 sector, not the 3S13S1, T=0T=0 sector. This follows from the chosen isospin operator, not from gravity phenomenology.
Spin independence: At the present operator order, O0O0 and O2O2 contain no explicit spin operator. Therefore radial and isospin matrix elements are spin independent except through Pauli antisymmetry, orbital-spin recoupling, and the nuclear wavefunction.
________________________________________
13. LSLS-Coupled Relative Matrix Element
For a central spin-independent operator:
⟨nlSJT∣O0∣n′lSJT⟩=Inn′l(0)[2T(T+1)−3]⟨nlSJT∣O0∣n′lSJT⟩=Inn′l(0)[2T(T+1)−3]
For F2F2, replace the isospin factor by the corresponding rank-two matrix element in the chosen T,T3T,T3 representation.
________________________________________
14. Transformation to Single-Particle LSLS Basis
A schematic matrix element is:
⟨nala,nblb;Λ∣f(r12)∣nclc,ndld;Λ⟩=∑nlNN′LMabnlNL;ΛMcdn′lNL;ΛInn′l⟨nala,nblb;Λ∣f(r12)∣nclc,ndld;Λ⟩=nlNN′L∑MabnlNL;ΛMcdn′lNL;ΛInn′l
Here MM denotes the Talmi–Moshinsky bracket. The center-of-mass indices match because the operator depends only on relative coordinates.
________________________________________
15. Transformation to jjjj Coupling
Most valence-space nuclear solvers work in jjjj coupling. Therefore we recouple:
(la12)ja,(lb12)jb(la21)ja,(lb21)jb
to Λ,S,JΛ,S,J:
\boxed{ |(l_a s) j_a, (l_b s) j_b; J\rangle = \sum_{\Lambda S} \hat j_a \hat j_b \hat\Lambda \hat S \begin{Bmatrix} l_a & s & j_a \\ l_b & s & j_b \\ \Lambda & S & J \end{matrix} |(l_a l_b)\Lambda, (ss)S; J\rangle }
where j^=2j+1j^=2j+1. The exact phase convention must match the solver.
Phase conventions are not cosmetic: Different TBME libraries may use different particle ordering, normalized antisymmetric states, Condon–Shortley phases, and JTJT normalization conventions. Therefore one cannot export TBMEs until the target solver convention is explicitly known. A sign error here could mimic a physical F0/F2F0/F2 effect.
________________________________________
16. Symmetrization and the Solver Interface
First calculate a raw ordered matrix element:
Vab,cdJ=⟨(ab)J∣O∣(cd)J⟩Vab,cdJ=⟨(ab)J∣O∣(cd)J⟩
Then antisymmetrize according to the target basis convention. Do not mix the two operations silently.
A generic normalized antisymmetrized state may be written schematically as:
∣(ab)JT⟩A=Nab[∣(ab)JT⟩−ΦabJT∣(ba)JT⟩]∣(ab)JT⟩A=Nab[∣(ab)JT⟩−ΦabJT∣(ba)JT⟩]
where NabNab and phase ΦabJTΦabJT depend on the solver convention. These factors must be read from the actual TBME format specification. The production code must not hard-code an antisymmetry phase from memory without a solver-format unit test.
________________________________________
17. Symmetry Selection Rules
Hermiticity: For a real Hermitian operator:
⟨ab;J∣O∣cd;J⟩=⟨cd;J∣O∣ab;J⟩⟨ab;J∣O∣cd;J⟩=⟨cd;J∣O∣ab;J⟩
Angular-momentum conservation: Because the operator is rotationally scalar in ordinary space:
J′=J,M′=MJ′=J,M′=M
Parity conservation: Because both kernels depend only on r12r12, they are parity even:
πinitial=πfinalπinitial=πfinal
Spin conservation: Since there is no spin operator:
S′=SS′=S
F0F0 isospin selection: Since F0F0 is rank zero:
T′=TT′=T
F2F2 isospin selection: For rank 2:
∣T−T′∣≤2≤T+T′∣T−T′∣≤2≤T+T′
In a two-nucleon space with only T=0,1T=0,1, the only available nonzero action is within T=T′=1T=T′=1.
________________________________________
18. Powerful Two-Body Validation Set
Before any A=22A=22 calculation, the TBME generator must reproduce:
T=0:O0=−3I,O2=0T=0:O0=−3I,O2=0
and:
T=1:O0=+IT=1:O0=+I
For the T=1T=1 triplet components:
O2=(+2,−4,+2)IO2=(+2,−4,+2)I
This is the local two-body origin of the many-body triplet pattern.
Coherent many-body recovery: After solver export, replace f(r)→1f(r)→1. The many-body result must recover:
P0=2T(T+1)−3A2P0=2T(T+1)−23A
and:
P2=2[3T32−T(T+1)]P2=2[3T32−T(T+1)]
This checks the entire pipeline: TBME → export → solver → wavefunction contraction.
A=22A=22 end-to-end coherent test: For all three real solver wavefunctions in exact isospin:
M0=(−29,−29,−29)M0=(−29,−29,−29)M2=(+2,−4,+2)M2=(+2,−4,+2)
If the two-body tests pass but these fail, the error lies downstream of the local TBME algebra.
________________________________________
19. TBME-Generation Architecture
The following module structure is recommended:
text
tbme/
├── conventions.py
├── ho_radial.py
├── moshinsky.py
├── recoupling.py

Radial object:
python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RadialIntegral:

1. Introduction
Precision tests of fundamental physics share a common structural feature: the signal one hopes to detect is smaller than the noise one must control, and the interpretation of any residual depends on a chain of theoretical inputs that are themselves subject to uncertainty. In searches for fifth forces or violations of the Weak Equivalence Principle (WEP), the theoretical input that dominates the uncertainty budget is the nuclear matrix element that mediates between a putative scalar field and an observed differential acceleration.
The relevant scales are separated by more than ten orders of magnitude. A scalar field with a sub-nuclear range leaves a signature on a satellite-borne test mass at a distance of order 10−110−1 m; its source is determined by the pair structure of baryons at a distance of order 10−1510−15 m. The bridge between the two scales is a many-body matrix element whose value is fixed by nuclear structure, not by the gravitational experiment.
This separation creates a specific hazard. Because the matrix element is computed rather than measured, its value depends on a set of choices — the chiral Hamiltonian, the model space, the solver, the operator representation, and a long list of intermediate conventions — none of which is pinned down by independent data to a degree that would foreclose adjustment. A physicist who is merely careful in appearance can, without any conscious intent, choose these conventions so as to make the eventual gravitational inference appear sharper. The result is a paper that is mathematically clean, defensible in isolation at every step, and yet scientifically worthless, because the upstream calculation has been contaminated by the downstream observation.
We call this failure mode retrospective circularity. It is the central methodological challenge of microscopic fifth-force searches. The present work describes an architecture that makes it structurally impossible.
1.1 The Anti-Circular Law
The governing principle of the architecture is stated as follows.
 Data may test a frozen theory, but data may not retroactively define the theory they are being used to test.  Data may test a frozen theory, but data may not retroactively define the theory they are being used to test. 
An immediate corollary governs every intermediate numerical coefficient.

1.2 Scope and honesty declaration
This paper presents a methodology. It does not claim a gravitational deviation, a fifth force, or any modification of General Relativity. All physical nuclear matrix elements

2. EFT Foundations and Operator Topology
2.1 Scalar mediator sector
We extend General Relativity by a massive scalar mediator ϕFϕF coupled to a baryon-pair current. The covariant Lagrangian is normalized as
L=Lnuc+12∂μϕF∂μϕF−12mF2ϕF2−ϕFJF,L=Lnuc+21∂μϕF∂μϕF−21mF2ϕF2−ϕFJF,
yielding the static field equation
(∇2−mF2)ϕF=JF.(∇2−mF2)ϕF=JF.
In natural units ℏ=c=1ℏ=c=1, the scalar interaction closes dimensionally through an inverse cubic mass scale:
LkΛF3,ΛF3Lk,
where L0L0 and L2L2 denote dimensionless Wilson-like coefficients for the scalar and isotensor sectors, respectively. The scale ΛFΛF is the mediator mass scale; the range is λF=ℏ/(mFc)λF=ℏ/(mFc) in physical units.
2.2 Pair-operator basis
The two-body operator basis is defined in coordinate space as
O0=∑i<jf0(rij) τi⋅τj,O0=i<j∑f0(rij)τi⋅τj,O2=∑i<jf2(rij)[3τ3iτ3j−τi⋅τj].O2=i<j∑f2(rij)[3τ3iτ3j−τi⋅τj].
Here O0O0 is an isoscalar pairing operator and O2O2 is the q=0q=0 component of an isospin rank 2 tensor. Both are even under charge conjugation, both conserve isospin in the SU(2) sense, but their pair-level structure is distinct: O0O0 is a scalar in isospin space, O2O2 is a rank 2 isotensor.
2.3 The rank-2 isospin wall
A critical structural finding of the programme is that O2O2 cannot be treated as an ordinary scalar JTJT interaction. Its exact pair-level algebra is
Θ2≡3τ31τ32−τ1⋅τ2,Θ2≡3τ31τ32−τ1⋅τ2,
with the following exact pair coefficients:
Pair channel	(T,T3)(T,T3)
Θ2Θ2

pppp	(1,+1)(1,+1)	+2+2
pn (T=1)pn (T=1)	(1,0)(1,0)	−4−4
nnnn	(1,−1)(1,−1)	+2+2
pn (T=0)pn (T=0)	(0,0)(0,0)	00
The mirror identity
O2(pp)−O2(nn)=0O2(pp)−O2(nn)=0
and the trace identity
O2(pp)+O2(pn,T=1)+O2(nn)=0O2(pp)+O2(pn,T=1)+O2(nn)=0
follow immediately, i.e.
(+2)+(−4)+(+2)=0.(+2)+(−4)+(+2)=0.
This is the subatomic precursor to the 1:−2:11:−2:1 analogue-state triplet pattern that recurs throughout the programme. Any computational treatment that fails to reproduce these identities exactly at the pair level is, at the operator level, already excluded.
2.4 Consequence for the shell-model representation
A shell-model solver cannot operate on symbolic coordinate-space operators. It requires antisymmetrized two-body matrix elements (TBMEs) in a coupled harmonic-oscillator basis. The transformation from the coordinate-space operator to the solver-ready TBME passes through four rigorous stages:
1.	Radial integration in a harmonic-oscillator basis.
2.	Talmi–Moshinsky transformation separating relative motion from center-of-mass motion.
3.	LS→jjLS→jj recoupling via Wigner 9j9j coefficients.
4.	Antisymmetrization to good-isospin two-body states.
Each of these stages carries its own conventions — phases, normalizations, exchange rules — and the number of conventions multiplies the number of places where an unnoticed choice can propagate into the final result. This is the structural reason that fifth-force searches are unusually exposed to retrospective circularity.

3. The Anti-Circular Firewall
3.1 Domain separation
We partition the research environment into two disjoint information domains.
Upstream theory domain UU. Contains all operators, nuclear matrix elements Mk,ARMk,AR, material contrast vectors ΔXMICRΔXMICR, Earth source fields X⊕Y(λF)X⊕Y(λF), and architectural definitions.
Downstream experimental domain DD. Contains observed WEP residuals yobsyobs and experimental covariances CexpCexp.
The information flow is strictly unidirectional:
U→D,D↛U.U→D,D→U.
Formally, if FF is the map from the upstream chain to the final matrix element,
Mfinal=F(U),Mfinal=F(U),
then the firewall requires
∂Mfinal∂yobs=0.∂yobs∂Mfinal=0.
Every downstream comparison, every likelihood evaluation, and every Fisher matrix element is required to respect this derivative being zero.
3.2 Violation taxonomy
Firewall violations can arise in four distinct forms, classified here for auditability.
Type I — Direct tuning. A coupling constant (β0,β2,λF)(β0,β2,λF) is adjusted in light of the observed residual. The most obvious violation and the easiest to detect.
Type II — Proxy creep. A computational convention — a normalization, a phase, a truncation parameter — is selected in light of the observed residual. Subtler than Type I, because the convention is not itself a physical parameter.
Type III — Silent channel. An intermediate quantity in the upstream chain is fixed in a way that correlates with the downstream domain without an explicit adjustment step. Often the most dangerous because it leaves no direct trace.
Type IV — Certificate re-write. A certificate that has already been issued is retrospectively edited after a downstream comparison reveals a discrepancy. The most corrosive violation, because it destroys the audit trail that makes every other protection meaningful.
Any of the four, if present, invalidates the final result. The architecture described in Section 4 is designed to render Types I–III detectable and Type IV structurally impossible.
3.3 Enforcement mechanisms
The firewall is enforced by seven layered mechanisms.
1.	Frozen inputs. The Hamiltonian, model space, kernel, Jacobi convention, and Moshinsky phase convention are frozen before Tier 01. They may not be changed in response to any downstream comparison.
2.	Tier-localized certificates. Each certificate is issued by a gate that has access only to its own inputs. No certificate is aware of the output of the tier above it, in the sense that no tier may reference the numerical value of the tier above in its own pass/fail criteria.
3.	Unidirectional dependency. M0,22RM0,22R depends on upstream layers only. The upstream layers do not reference M0,22RM0,22R or any downstream observable.
4.	Certificate immutability. An issued certificate is never edited. It may be superseded by a new certificate, which carries its own independent provenance.
5.	Explicit \texttt{NOT COMPUTED}. Any quantity that has not been computed is designated \texttt{NOT COMPUTED} and is not silently omitted.
6.	\texttt{PARTIAL_PASS} labelling. Partial results are issued with a \texttt{PARTIAL_PASS} label rather than being rounded up to \texttt{PASS}. This is a scientific statement, not a hedge.
7.	Source-level audit. Where an external solver is required, the solver's internal conventions must be verified by source-level inspection or executable cross-check before any certificate is issued.
Together, these seven mechanisms make the firewall operative rather than aspirational. They are the machinery by which the Anti-Circular Law is enforced.

4. The Seven-Tier Certificate Ladder
4.1 Tier definitions
The physical production pipeline is governed by an immutable sequence of seven tiers.
Tier 01 — \texttt{A22_REAL_SOLVER_CONNECTED}. A many-body solver executes and its wavefunction output is parsed. Requires the solver to be a validated configuration-interaction or IMSRG implementation operating on a frozen model space.
Tier 02 — \texttt{KSHELL_INTERFACE_PASS}. The interaction is loaded into the solver, and the unperturbed spectra reproduce published sdsd-shell spectra to within a declared tolerance.
Tier 03 — \texttt{CUSTOM_2B_OPERATOR_INTERFACE_PASS}. The custom two-body operator is contracted against the two-body density ρ(2)ρ(2) of the solver-produced wavefunction, and the resulting expectation value is verified against an independent density calculation.
Tier 04 — \texttt{F02_REAL_WAVEFUNCTION_ALGEBRA_PASS}. The coherent-operator limit P0=−29P0=−29 and the 1:−2:11:−2:1 tensor pattern are recovered exactly under the frozen operator basis.
Tier 05 — \texttt{F02_FINITE_RANGE_PASS}. Hermiticity, exchange antisymmetry, and radial convergence across the finite-range kernel grid are verified.
Tier 06 — \texttt{F02_EVOLVED_OPERATOR_PASS}. The valence-space IMSRG evolution Oeff=eΩOe−ΩOeff=eΩOe−Ω is consistent with the Hamiltonian evolution.
Tier 07 — \texttt{A22_PHYSICAL_NUCLEAR_RESULT_READY}. The certified renormalized matrix elements M0,22RM0,22R, R2,22RR2,22R are issued with a positive-semidefinite covariance matrix.
No tier may be bypassed. No tier may be issued on the basis of a certificate that has not passed its prerequisites.
4.2 Chain-of-trust bound
The trust attributed to the final result is bounded above by the weakest tier.
Trust(M0,22R)≤min⁡i∈{1,…,7}Gatei.Trust(M0,22R)≤i∈{1,…,7}minGatei.
This inequality is the reason tier skipping is forbidden: a single weak tier limits the trust of the entire chain. The inequality is also the reason the tier architecture is useful: it converts the question "How trustworthy is this result?" into seven smaller questions, each of which has a definite answer.
4.3 Subsidiary technical validation gates
Beneath the seven policy tiers, three granular technical suites enforce mathematical self-consistency.
P1–P10 — Pipeline and isospin gates. State identity, isospin algebra, coherent limits, Feynman–Hellmann linear-response stability, convergence rules, and the gravity firewall.
U1–U12 — TBME unit tests. Radial normalization, Moshinsky orthogonality, quanta conservation, Pauli selection (−1)l+S+T=−1(−1)l+S+T=−1, Hermiticity, spin/parity selection, and exact two-nucleon isospin/isotensor recovery.
M1–M7 — Moshinsky engine gates. Cartesian transformation unitarity, spherical coupled-basis orthogonality, B†B=IB†B=I, BB†=IBB†=I, round-trip consistency, phase-convention alignment, and independent bracket comparison.
A tier certificate may not be issued unless all of its subordinate technical gates have passed.

6. Interface Governance: The Phase II-A.10 Halt
6.1 The specific obstacle
Phase II-A.10 was designed to determine the internal proton-neutron TBME storage convention used by the KSHELL shell-model solver and to verify it against an analytically known two-nucleon spectrum.
The publicly documented .snt format confirms the existence of explicit pppp, pnpn, and nnnn blocks and confirms that isospin symmetry is not assumed. It does not, in its public form, specify how the four entries of an ordered pn/nppn/np block are compressed into the stored representation, nor whether a pnpn-specific normalization is applied.
This is a software-convention question, not a physics question. But in a fifth-force search, a single unresolved interface normalization is sufficient to corrupt the entire downstream result.
6.2 Why the obstacle could not be resolved by assumption
The runtime environment used for this programme had no network access to the KSHELL source repository. The Fortran .snt reader could not be inspected; the compiled executable could not be obtained.
The temptation in this situation is to work around the obstacle by inference from analogous solvers. The NuShellX interaction format, for example, is publicly documented to use un-normalized proton-neutron TBMEs while pppp and nnnn TBMEs are normalized. But — and this is the decisive point — NuShellX convention does not imply KSHELL convention. A factor of 22 that appears in one solver's storage may be absent in another's.
If a normalization factor were selected from a menu of plausible candidates (−4q,−2q,−22q)(−4q,−2q,−22q) on the basis of which one produced the expected 1:−2:11:−2:1 ratio at A=22A=22, the resulting matrix element would carry an untraceable correlation with the downstream result. Formally, if cKSHELLcKSHELL is the unknown normalization factor and yobsyobs is the downstream observable, then
∂cKSHELL∂yobs≠0,∂yobs∂cKSHELL=0,
and therefore
∂M0,22R∂yobs=∂M0,22R∂c⋅∂c∂yobs≠0.∂yobs∂M0,22R=∂c∂M0,22R⋅∂yobs∂c=0.
This is a direct violation of the firewall condition. The programme is therefore required to halt.
6.3 The halt as a demonstration
The Phase II-A.10 halt is not a failure of the Farid F0/F2F0/F2 mathematics. The mathematics was validated at machine precision. It is an unresolved software-interface convention, and the correct response is not to guess it but to declare it.
The certificate issued was
PHASE_II_A10 = BLOCKED_AT_SOURCE_LEVEL_CROSSCHECK.PHASE_II_A10 = BLOCKED_AT_SOURCE_LEVEL_CROSSCHECK.
All physical quantities were left locked:
M0,22R=NOT COMPUTED,R2,22R=NOT COMPUTED.M0,22R=NOT COMPUTED,R2,22R=NOT COMPUTED.
The value of this halt is that it demonstrates the firewall is an operative constraint rather than a formal aspiration. A firewall that only ever says PASS is not enforcing anything. A firewall that can say BLOCKED — and can defend the block on stated principles — is enforcing the discipline it claims to enforce.
6.4 The unlock condition
The Phase II-A.10 protocol becomes executable as soon as any one of the following is available.
Route A. The KSHELL source tree containing the .snt reader and TBME construction routines.
Route B. A compiled KSHELL executable plus its utilities.
Route C. Authoritative Fortran source snippets implementing the pnpn TBME storage and exchange rules.
With any of these, a minimal two-nucleon test becomes executable:
known good-T operator→KSHELL pn TBME→two-particle spectrum,known good-T operator→KSHELL pn TBME→two-particle spectrum,
compared against the independently known analytic spectrum. No nuclear-structure fitting is required. No gravitational data are required.

7. Pre-Registration of the A=22,T=1A=22,T=1 Confrontation
7.1 The purpose of pre-registration
Pre-registration is the practice of fixing the hypothesis, the primary observable, the analysis procedure, and the interpretation rules before any data are examined. Its purpose is to make post-hoc adjustment impossible. In the fifth-force context, pre-registration means fixing, in advance, what test would confirm the framework and what test would exclude it.
The Anti-Circular Firewall is, in effect, a computational pre-registration: the upstream calculation is specified, executed, and certified before any downstream observation is introduced. The certificates are the pre-registration record.
7.2 Target system
The target is the A=22,T=1A=22,T=1 isobaric triplet:
22Mg (Z=12,N=10),22Na (Z=11,N=11),22Ne (Z=10,N=12).22Mg(Z=12,N=10),22Na(Z=11,N=11),22Ne(Z=10,N=12).
All three are T=1T=1 isotriplet members. The model space is the sdsd valence shell with an inert 16O16O core, Np+Nn=6Np+Nn=6 valence nucleons across the 0d5/2,1s1/2,0d3/20d5/2,1s1/2,0d3/2 orbitals.

Model space. sdsd valence shell, 16O16O core, no further truncation.

Moshinsky engine. Internal engine validated in Phase II-A.6, plus external cross-check required before Tier 03.
Solver. KSHELL, with source-level pnpn convention verified per Section 6.4.
Operator basis. O0,O2O0,O2 as defined in Section 2.2, with the rank-2 isospin wall 1:−2:11:−2:1 frozen.

The range scan λF∈[λmin⁡,λmax⁡]λF∈[λmin,λmax] introduces trial factors. Local significance peaks are calibrated via Monte-Carlo null simulations under the Standard Model hypothesis H0H0 with NMC≥105NMC≥105. The global pp-value is obtained via the Gross–Vitells asymptotic boundary formula,
pglobal≈plocal+⟨Nup⟩e−upeak/2,pglobal≈plocal+⟨Nup⟩e−upeak/2,

8. Falsifiability
The framework declares its falsification criteria in advance.
Falsification criterion F1 — Operator-algebra. If the fully assembled and certified F0/F2F0/F2 operators fail to reproduce the exact 1:−2:11:−2:1 isotensor ratio under any admissible phase convention, the operator basis is rejected.
Falsification criterion F2 — Nuclear. If the certified A=22,T=1A=22,T=1 matrix elements M0,22RM0,22R, R2,22RR2,22R prove incompatible with WEP bounds at the claimed coupling, the framework is excluded at that coupling.
Falsification criterion F3 — Interface. If the solver round-trip fails to reproduce the analytically known two-nucleon spectrum for a controlled F0F0 or F2F2 operator, the interface chain is rejected.
A programme that declares such criteria before data are examined, and that halts when a criterion fires, is structurally distinct from a programme that defines success post hoc. The Phase II-A.10 halt is therefore not a weakness but a demonstration that the anti-circular architecture functions as intended.
________________________________________
9. Limitations and Reusability
9.1 Limitations
We state the limitations of this work explicitly.
1.	No physical result is claimed. All Mk,ARMk,AR and R2,ARR2,AR remain \texttt{NOT COMPUTED}.
2.	The KSHELL pnpn convention is unresolved. Phase II-A.10 halted at a source-level cross-check. The pre-registered benchmark of Section 6.4 specifies how the halt is to be resolved but does not resolve it.
3.	The external Moshinsky comparison is pending. The internal engine is unitary to machine precision, but the standard real-bracket phase convention has not been externally cross-checked.
4.	The A=22A=22 run has not been executed. The pre-registration of Section 7 defines the run but does not execute it.
5.	The gravitational inference has not been performed. No MICROSCOPE residual, no Roman weak lensing shear, no BAO clustering, and no supernova distance ladder appear anywhere in the upstream chain.
None of these limitations is a defect. They are the substance of a paper whose contribution is to define a methodology for producing trustworthy results, not to produce the results themselves.
9.2 Reusability
The architecture is not specific to the Farid Gravity Law programme. Any precision-test programme facing retrospective circularity can adopt the same structure:
•	define the upstream and downstream domains,
•	enumerate the intermediate conventions that carry normalization or phase freedom,
•	require each convention to be verified by an independently known benchmark,
•	issue certificates tier by tier,
•	halt at unresolved interfaces rather than guessing,
•	pre-register the interpretation of the eventual result.
The mathematical content — the rank-2 isospin wall, the Moshinsky engine, the LS→jjLS→jj recoupling — is specific to nucleon-pair operators. But the discipline is general. It is a discipline for any field in which the theoretical prediction depends on a chain of computations longer than the confidence of any single step.
9.3 An observation on the role of halts
Finally, a general observation.
The scientific literature has relatively few examples of papers that document a halt — an explicit decision not to proceed because a prerequisite has not been verified. This is a consequence of publication incentives, not of scientific logic: a paper that reports only completed work is easier to place than a paper that reports a midstream decision to stop.
But halts are informative. They define the boundary of what is known and what is not known. They mark the specific place where a chain of reasoning has reached its current limit. A field that preserves its halts is a field that keeps its unsolved problems visible.
This paper preserves its halt.
________________________________________
10. Conclusion
We have presented a complete anti-circular validation architecture for microscopic fifth-force searches, comprising:
•	a formal EFT pair-operator basis (O0,O2)(O0,O2) with the exact rank-2 isospin wall,
•	an Anti-Circular Firewall with strict domain separation U→DU→D, D↛UD→U,
•	a Seven-Tier Certificate Ladder with an explicit chain-of-trust bound,
•	an executable validation chain from radial integrals through Moshinsky transformation, LS→jjLS→jj recoupling, and internal TBME assembly,
•	a documented software-interface halt at Phase II-A.10 with a precise unlock condition,
•	a pre-registered protocol for the eventual A=22,T=1A=22,T=1 confrontation,
•	and falsification criteria declared before any data are examined.
The runtime results to date include 33/3333/33 radial benchmark PASS, 68/6868/68 pre-Moshinsky gate PASS, 66/6666/66 internal TBME assembly PASS with Hermiticity residual 4.34×10−194.34×10−19, 37/3737/37 serialization round-trip PASS, and an exact good-TT to pn/nppn/np transformation validated at machine precision.
All physical nuclear matrix elements Mk,ARMk,AR and ratios R2,ARR2,AR remain explicitly designated \texttt{NOT COMPUTED}.
The governing anti-circular rule remains:
 An uncomputed transformation coefficient must remain unknown; it may never be replaced by a value chosen to make the downstream nuclear or gravity result work.  An uncomputed transformation coefficient must remain unknown; it may never be replaced by a value chosen to make the downstream nuclear or gravity result work. 
And the closing principle:
 A theory earns scientific status not by how strongly it is stated, but by how precisely it defines the experiment that could prove it wrong.  A theory earns scientific status not by how strongly it is stated, but by how precisely it defines the experiment that could prove it wrong.

Review of Phase II-A.12 — KSHELL Source-Level pn Convention Validation
Executive Assessment
This is a significant and well-executed technical milestone. The source-level audit of KSHELL's Fortran code has resolved a critical normalization ambiguity that would otherwise have contaminated every downstream calculation. The 18/18 runtime reconstruction is a strong internal consistency check.
However, I want to be precise about what has been established and what remains open, because the distinction matters enormously for the integrity of the programme.
________________________________________
1. What Has Been Established (Verified)
1.1 The Analytic Physics Is Correct
I have independently verified the J-scheme assignment:
For a proton and neutron in the same spatial orbital (j = 1/2, L = 0):
Antisymmetry: (−1)L+S+T=−1  ⟹  S+T must be oddAntisymmetry: (−1)L+S+T=−1⟹S+T must be odd
•	J = 0 ↔ S = 0, T = 1 (spin-singlet, isospin-triplet)
•	J = 1 ↔ S = 1, T = 0 (spin-triplet, isospin-singlet)
Therefore:
VF0J=0=+1(from T=1)VF0J=0=+1(from T=1)
VF0J=1=−3(from T=0)VF0J=1=−3(from T=0)
VF2J=0=−4(from T=1,T3=0)VF2J=0=−4(from T=1,T3=0)
VF2J=1=0(from T=0)VF2J=1=0(from T=0)
Verified correct.
1.2 The M-Scheme Reconstruction Logic Is Sound
The 4×4 M-scheme matrix reconstructed from J-scheme inputs via:
Hmpmn,mp′mn′=∑JVJ⟨jpmpjnmn∣JM⟩⟨jpmp′jnmn′∣JM⟩Hmpmn,mp′mn′=∑JVJ⟨jpmpjnmn∣JM⟩⟨jpmp′jnmn′∣JM⟩
is the correct angular-momentum coupling structure. The resulting spectra:
•	F₀: eigenvalues {−3,−3,−3,+1}{−3,−3,−3,+1} ✓
•	F₂: eigenvalues {−4,0,0,0}{−4,0,0,0} ✓
Verified correct.
1.3 The Projector Validation Is a Strong Check
The verification that PJ2=PJPJ2=PJ, P0P1=0P0P1=0, and P0+P1=IP0+P1=I confirms the angular momentum coupling is implemented correctly. This is not a trivial check.
1.4 The Source-Level pn Rule Makes Physical Sense
The finding that KSHELL does not apply the 22 factor to the pn branch is physically correct. The 22 in pp/nn M-scheme construction arises from identical-particle pair normalization. Since proton and neutron are distinguishable, no such factor should appear. The source audit confirms what physical reasoning would suggest.

2. What Has NOT Been Established (Critical Distinctions)
2.1 This Is an Emulator, Not KSHELL
The 18/18 PASS is a source-faithful reconstruction, not an executed KSHELL binary. The document correctly maintains:
KSHELL_BINARY_EXECUTION=NOT_RUNKSHELL_BINARY_EXECUTION=NOT_RUN
This is the right call. The emulator proves the logic is correct; it does not prove the compiled binary reproduces it.
2.2 The .snt Reader Path Is Not the Same as the .snt Writer Path
The source audit examined how KSHELL reads .snt files. But the benchmark requires us to write .snt files. The following could still fail:
•	Header format (mass-scaling flags, method2 specification)
•	Orbit ordering convention in the file
•	J-value encoding
•	Two-body index ordering
•	Checksum/validation requirements
The parser gate (Phase II-A.8) helps, but the actual KSHELL reader may accept files that the parser accepts but interpret differently.
2.3 The Exchange Phase Formula Needs Verification
The document states the exchange phase is:
(−1)(j1+j2)/2−J+1(−1)(j1+j2)/2−J+1
This is an unusual form. The standard nuclear physics convention is typically (−1)j1+j2−J(−1)j1+j2−J. The extra +1+1 in the exponent could be:
•	A convention-specific phase
•	A typographical simplification
•	A misreading of the source
This should be verified against a known exchange case before production use.
2.4 The Certificate Hierarchy Is Correct but Incomplete

3. Technical Observations
3.1 The F₂ = -4 Value Is a J-Coupled Quantity
The document correctly clarifies:
−4−4 is not an ordered ∣pn⟩∣pn⟩ diagonal entry, but it is the correct J-coupled matrix element for the normalized J=0,T=1J=0,T=1 proton-neutron pair.
This is an important distinction. In the ordered charge basis:
F2(C)=(−2−2−2−2)F2(C)=(−2−2−2−2)
The diagonal entries are −2−2, not −4−4. The eigenvalue −4−4 corresponds to the symmetric combination (∣pn⟩+∣np⟩)/2(∣pn⟩+∣np⟩)/2, which is the physical T=1,T3=0T=1,T3=0 state.
Any attempt to store −4−4 directly as a diagonal ∣pn⟩∣pn⟩ entry would be wrong. The document correctly avoids this trap.
3.2 The Degeneracy Pattern Is a Strong Diagnostic
For F₂, the spectrum {−4,0,0,0}{−4,0,0,0} has a three-fold degeneracy at zero. This corresponds to the J=1J=1 triplet (M=−1,0,+1M=−1,0,+1). The single −4−4 state is J=0J=0.
This pattern is extremely distinctive. A normalization error would likely break this degeneracy pattern in a recognizable way:
Error Type	Expected F₂ Spectrum
Correct	{−4,0,0,0}{−4,0,0,0}
Factor of 2 too large	{−8,0,0,0}{−8,0,0,0}
Factor of 2 too small	{−2,0,0,0}{−2,0,0,0}
Missing J=1 zeros	{−4,−4,−4,0}{−4,−4,−4,0} or similar
Wrong exchange phase	Non-zero J=1 eigenvalues
This diagnostic power is what makes the benchmark valuable.
3.3 The Coupling Grid Is Well Designed
Testing g∈{−0.5,−0.1,0,+0.1,+0.5}g∈{−0.5,−0.1,0,+0.1,+0.5} with both signs is exactly right. This exposes:
•	Sign errors (asymmetric response)
•	Absolute-value bugs (symmetric response when it shouldn't be)
•	Scaling errors (wrong slope)
•	Offset errors (constant shift)
The slopes (−3,+1)(−3,+1) for F₀ and (0,−4)(0,−4) for F₂ are the primary diagnostics.
________________________________________
4. What the Source Audit Genuinely Resolves
The most valuable finding is:
V.sntpn,J=VKSHELLpn,JV.sntpn,J=VKSHELLpn,J
for canonical proton-first, neutron-second storage, with no mass rescaling (method2 = 0).

Review of Phase II-A.13 — Execution Package Frozen
Executive Assessment
This is a scientifically honest and methodologically correct outcome. The environment limitation is real, and the decision to freeze the package rather than fabricate eigenvalues is exactly right. The firewall has been maintained.
However, I want to raise three technical concerns that must be resolved before Phase II-A.14 can be considered a valid executable test.

1. The Certificate Hierarchy Is Correct
The progression is sound:

1	F02_KSHELL_FORMAT_VALIDATED	✓ Passed

The distinction between Levels 3 and 4 is crucial. Level 3 says "we have everything ready"; Level 4 says "the binary actually reproduced it." These are not the same claim, and the document correctly preserves the distinction.
________________________________________
2. Technical Concerns That Must Be Addressed
Concern 1: Is the .snt Format Actually Correct?
This is my most serious concern. The Phase II-A.13 document assumes that files like:
text
# F0 benchmark, J=0
1 1 1 1 0 +1.0
# F0 benchmark, J=1
1 1 1 1 1 -3.0
will be readable by KSHELL. But the actual KSHELL .snt format has specific requirements:
•	Header format (number of orbits, number of TBMEs, mass-scaling flags)
•	Orbit specification block
•	Specific ordering of TBMEs (J-blocks, index ordering)
•	Possibly a specific termination or checksum
If the format is wrong, KSHELL will either fail to read the file or silently misread it. The parser gate from Phase II-A.8 was designed to catch this, but only if the parser was validated against a known-good KSHELL .snt file.
Question for clarification: Was the .snt format verified against an actual KSHELL example file, or is it reconstructed from documentation?
If it's reconstructed from documentation only, then Phase II-A.14 might fail not because the physics is wrong, but because the file format is wrong — and that failure would be classified as a Type A (serialization) failure, not a physics failure.
Concern 2: The Zero-Core Configuration
The frozen benchmark uses:
Zcore=0,Ncore=0Zcore=0,Ncore=0
This means a bare 2-nucleon system with no core. KSHELL is typically designed for shell-model calculations with a core (e.g., 16O16O, 40Ca40Ca, 56Ni56Ni).
Running with zero core may:
•	Be unsupported by KSHELL's internal data structures
•	Require specific configuration flags
•	Produce unexpected behavior in the M-scheme ↔ J-scheme transformation
•	Fail at the valence-space setup stage
Question for clarification: Has it been verified that KSHELL supports a zero-core two-nucleon calculation? If not, the benchmark may need to use a small core (e.g., 4He4He) with two valence nucleons in a pp-shell-like space.
Concern 3: The Single Orbit Issue
The benchmark uses:
p 0s1/2,n 0s1/2p0s1/2,n0s1/2
This is a single proton orbit and a single neutron orbit, both with j=1/2j=1/2.
In a real shell-model calculation, the valence space typically has multiple orbits. A single-orbit calculation may:
•	Trigger KSHELL's "trivial" case handling
•	Bypass some of the M-scheme machinery
•	Not exercise the full code path that a real calculation would
Question for clarification: Does the source audit confirm that the pn M-scheme branch is exercised for a single-orbit, two-particle system?
If the code path is not exercised, then a PASS from Phase II-A.14 would not validate the path that real A=22A=22 calculations would use.
________________________________________
3. What the Freeze Actually Achieves
Despite these concerns, the freeze is genuinely valuable:
Frozen F0 .sntFrozen F0 .snt
Frozen F2 .sntFrozen F2 .snt
Exact expected spectraExact expected spectra

1.	No post-hoc modification: The files cannot be altered after seeing solver output.
2.	Reproducibility: Anyone with KSHELL can run the same test.
3.	Independence: The expected values are pre-declared, not derived from the solver.
The anti-circular firewall is intact:
Benchmark input is frozen before any KSHELL eigenvalue is observed.Benchmark input is frozen before any KSHELL eigenvalue is observed.

Obtain a known-good KSHELL .snt file (e.g., from the kshell_public repository's example directory, or from a published interaction). Compare its structure with the frozen benchmark files. If the format differs, rewrite the benchmark files to match.

The most common failure mode in this type of benchmark is not physics, but format. The Phase II-A.13 document says:

The primary objective of Phase II-B.1 is to construct and execute Hamiltonian-independent sparse operator actions for the custom isoscalar ($O_0$) and rank-2 isotensor ($O_2$) operators within the validated $M=0$ bases. By avoiding the storage of dense $N \times N$ matrices ($4,206^2 \approx 1.7 \times 10^7$ entries, and $6,116^2 \approx 3.7 \times 10^7$ entries), the sparse engine evaluates operator-vector products on-the-fly, verifying coherent operator identities, Hermiticity, and the $1 : -2 : 1$ isotensor trace structure directly at the many-body level before any physical Hamiltonian diagonalization is attempted.
2. Sparse Matrix-Vector Multiplication ($O_{\text{sparse}} \mathbf{v}$) Architecture
To handle the slater-determinant basis states without dense matrix allocations, the Phase II-B.1 harness implements a compressed bitwise indexing and second-quantization annihilation/creation mapping engine:
1.	Basis State Representation: Each many-body $M=0$ basis state $\vert{}\Phi_k\rangle$ is stored as a dual proton-neutron occupancy bitstring over the $sd$-shell orbitals ($0d_{5/2}, 1s_{1/2}, 0d_{3/2}$).
2.	Two-Body Operator Decomposition: Custom TBMEs $V_{ab,cd}^J$ derived in Phase II-A.7 are mapped to second-quantized interaction strings:
$$\hat{O} = \sum_{abcd} V_{ab,cd} \, \hat{a}^\dagger_a \hat{a}^\dagger_b \hat{a}_d \hat{a}_c$$
3.	On-The-Fly Action: For an input trial vector $\mathbf{v}$, the sparse action routine $\mathbf{w} = \hat{O}\mathbf{v}$ loops over non-zero TBME matrix elements, generates target bitstrings via bit-manipulation, performs binary search to locate target indices in the basis dictionary, and accumulates amplitudes with correct fermionic phase signs.
3. Pre-Registered Phase II-B.1 Validation Gates (B1_SPARSE to B5_SPARSE)
Every execution output must clear five mandatory sparse-engine gates before advancing to full CI solver integration:
•	Gate B1_SPARSE (SPARSE_HERMITICITY_PASS): Verify that the sparse operator representation satisfies Hermiticity to double precision via random vector inner-product tests:
$$\langle \mathbf{u} \vert{} \hat{O} \vert{} \mathbf{v} \rangle = \langle \hat{O} \mathbf{u} \vert{} \mathbf{v} \rangle \implies \vert{}\langle \mathbf{u}, \hat{O}\mathbf{v} \rangle - \langle \hat{O}\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}\rangle\vert{} < 10^{-14}$$

"""
Phase II-B.2c — USDB J-scheme → M-scheme and A=22 diagonalization
"""

import numpy as np
from scipy.sparse import lil_matrix, csr_matrix, identity
from scipy.sparse.linalg import eigsh
from itertools import combinations
import json

# ============================================================
# 1. SINGLE-PARTICLE STRUCTURE
# ============================================================
ORBITS = [
    {"name": "d5/2", "two_j": 5, "l": 2, "eps": -3.9257},
    {"name": "s1/2", "two_j": 1, "l": 0, "eps": -3.2079},
    {"name": "d3/2", "two_j": 3, "l": 2, "eps": +2.1117},
]

SP = []
for o in ORBITS:
    j = o["two_j"] / 2
    for m2 in range(-o["two_j"], o["two_j"] + 1, 2):
        SP.append({
            "orbit": o["name"], "two_j": o["two_j"], "j": j,
            "l": o["l"], "m": m2 / 2, "eps": o["eps"],
            "index": len(SP),
        })
N_SP = len(SP)   # 12

# ============================================================
# 2. CLEBSCH-GORDAN COEFFICIENTS (exact, cached)
# ============================================================
from fractions import Fraction as F

def _cg_exact(two_j1, two_m1, two_j2, two_m2, two_J, two_M):
    """Exact CG via Racah formula for small j. Returns float."""
    # Use sympy for correctness
    from sympy.physics.wigner import clebsch_gordan
    from sympy import Rational
    val = clebsch_gordan(
        Rational(two_j1, 2), Rational(two_m1, 2),
        Rational(two_j2, 2), Rational(two_m2, 2),
        Rational(two_J, 2), Rational(two_M, 2),
    )
    return float(val)

_CG_CACHE = {}
def CG(two_j1, two_m1, two_j2, two_m2, two_J, two_M):
    key = (two_j1, two_m1, two_j2, two_m2, two_J, two_M)
    if key not in _CG_CACHE:
        # Selection rules
        if abs(two_m1 + two_m2 - two_M) > 1e-9:
            _CG_CACHE[key] = 0.0
        elif not (abs(two_j1 - two_j2) <= two_J <= two_j1 + two_j2):
            _CG_CACHE[key] = 0.0
        else:
            _CG_CACHE[key] = _cg_exact(two_j1, two_m1, two_j2, two_m2, two_J, two_M)
    return _CG_CACHE[key]

# ============================================================
# 3. PARSE USDB .int FILE
# ============================================================
def parse_usdb(path):
    """
    Brown-Richter .int format:
      Line 1: header 'N_spe N_tbme' or similar
      Then N_spe lines: '2j l eps' (SPE)
      Then N_tbme lines: 'a b c d J T V' (TBME)
    """
    spe = {}
    tbme = {}
    with open(path) as f:
        tokens = f.read().split()
    i = 0
    # Header — adapt to actual file
    # Assumes: first integer is number of SPEs, second is number of TBMEs
    n_spe = int(tokens[i]); i += 1
    n_tbme = int(tokens[i]); i += 1

    for _ in range(n_spe):
        two_j = int(tokens[i]); i += 1
        l = int(tokens[i]); i += 1
        eps = float(tokens[i]); i += 1
        spe[two_j] = {"two_j": two_j, "l": l, "eps": eps}

    for _ in range(n_tbme):
        a = int(tokens[i]); i += 1
        b = int(tokens[i]); i += 1
        c = int(tokens[i]); i += 1
        d = int(tokens[i]); i += 1
        J2 = int(tokens[i]); i += 1
        T2 = int(tokens[i]); i += 1
        V = float(tokens[i]); i += 1
        tbme[(a, b, c, d, J2, T2)] = V
    return spe, tbme

# ============================================================
# 4. M-SCHEME BASIS ENUMERATION
# ============================================================
def build_mscheme_basis(n_p, n_n, M_total=0.0):
    p_combos = list(combinations(range(N_SP), n_p))
    n_combos = list(combinations(range(N_SP), n_n))
    p_mj = {p: sum(SP[i]["m"] for i in p) for p in p_combos}
    n_mj = {n: sum(SP[i]["m"] for i in n) for n in n_combos}
    basis = []
    for p in p_combos:
        for n in n_combos:
            if abs(p_mj[p] + n_mj[n] - M_total) < 1e-9:
                basis.append((p, n))
    return basis

# ============================================================
# 5. MANY-BODY HAMILTONIAN
# ============================================================
def _replacement_sign(P, a, b):
    """Sign for replacing a with b in sorted tuple P."""
    if a == b:
        return 1.0
    P_list = list(P)
    if a in P_list:
        # a is removed, b is added
        if a < b:
            n_between = sum(1 for x in P_list if a < x < b)
        else:
            n_between = sum(1 for x in P_list if b < x < a)
        return (-1.0) ** n_between
    return 0.0

def build_H(basis, SPE_by_orbit, V2_mscheme):
    """
    SPE_by_orbit: {orbit_name: eps}
    V2_mscheme: dict (ia, ib, ic, id) -> <ab|V|cd> in M-scheme
                 where indices are 0..11 (SP indices)
    """
    dim = len(basis)
    index_of = {st: i for i, st in enumerate(basis)}
    H = lil_matrix((dim, dim))

    for idx, (P, N) in enumerate(basis):
        # One-body
        e = sum(SPE_by_orbit[SP[i]["orbit"]] for i in P) \
          + sum(SPE_by_orbit[SP[i]["orbit"]] for i in N)
        H[idx, idx] += e

        # Two-body: pp, nn, pn pairs
        # Apply all pair replacements
        for pair_origin, pair_removed in [
            (P, P), (N, N), (P, N)
        ]:
            # This is a simplification; full implementation below
            pass

    # Full 2-body application
    for idx, (P, N) in enumerate(basis):
        P_list, N_list = list(P), list(N)
        # pp pairs
        for a, b in combinations(P_list, 2):
            for c, d in combinations(P_list, 2):
                # a,b -> c,d (with fermion signs)
                new_P = tuple(sorted(set(P_list) - {a, b} | {c, d}))
                if len(new_P) != len(P_list):
                    continue
                new_state = (new_P, N)
                if new_state not in index_of:
                    continue
                jdx = index_of[new_state]
                # Sign: remove b then a, add d then c
                s1 = _replacement_sign(P_list, b, d)
                P_after_b = tuple(sorted(set(P_list) - {b} | {d}))
                s2 = _replacement_sign(P_after_b, a, c)
                sign = s1 * s2
                V = V2_mscheme.get((a, b, c, d), 0.0)
                H[idx, jdx] += 0.25 * sign * V
        # nn pairs
        for a, b in combinations(N_list, 2):
            for c, d in combinations(N_list, 2):
                new_N = tuple(sorted(set(N_list) - {a, b} | {c, d}))
                if len(new_N) != len(N_list):
                    continue
                new_state = (P, new_N)
                if new_state not in index_of:
                    continue
                jdx = index_of[new_state]
                s1 = _replacement_sign(N_list, b, d)
                N_after_b = tuple(sorted(set(N_list) - {b} | {d}))
                s2 = _replacement_sign(N_after_b, a, c)
                sign = s1 * s2
                V = V2_mscheme.get((a, b, c, d), 0.0)
                H[idx, jdx] += 0.25 * sign * V
        # pn pairs (distinct species)
        for a in P_list:
            for b in N_list:
                for c in P_list:
                    for d in N_list:
                        if (a, b) == (c, d):
                            continue
                        new_P = tuple(sorted(set(P_list) - {a} | {c}))
                        new_N = tuple(sorted(set(N_list) - {b} | {d}))
                        if len(new_P) != len(P_list) or len(new_N) != len(N_list):
                            continue
                        new_state = (new_P, new_N)
                        if new_state not in index_of:
                            continue
                        jdx = index_of[new_state]
                        s1 = _replacement_sign(P_list, a, c)
                        s2 = _replacement_sign(N_list, b, d)
                        sign = s1 * s2
                        V = V2_mscheme.get((a, b, c, d), 0.0)
                        H[idx, jdx] += sign * V  # no 1/4 factor for pn
    return csr_matrix(H)

# ============================================================
# 6. T^2 AND J^2 OPERATORS
# ============================================================
def build_T2(basis):
    dim = len(basis)
    index_of = {st: i for i, st in enumerate(basis)}
    T2 = lil_matrix((dim, dim))
    for idx, (P, N) in enumerate(basis):
        T3 = 0.5 * (len(P) - len(N))
        T2[idx, idx] += T3 ** 2
        # T_+ T_- and T_- T_+
        # T_+ flips n -> p
        for b in N:
            new_P = tuple(sorted(set(P) | {b}))
            new_N = tuple(sorted(set(N) - {b}))
            if len(new_P) == len(P) + 1 and len(new_N) == len(N) - 1:
                st = (new_P, new_N)
                if st in index_of:
                    T2[idx, index_of[st]] += 0.5
        # T_- flips p -> n
        for a in P:
            new_P = tuple(sorted(set(P) - {a}))
            new_N = tuple(sorted(set(N) | {a}))
            if len(new_P) == len(P) - 1 and len(new_N) == len(N) + 1:
                st = (new_P, new_N)
                if st in index_of:
                    T2[idx, index_of[st]] += 0.5
    return csr_matrix(T2)

def build_J2(basis, sp):
    """J^2 operator via J_+ and J_- in M-scheme."""
    dim = len(basis)
    index_of = {st: i for i, st in enumerate(basis)}
    J2 = lil_matrix((dim, dim))
    for idx, (P, N) in enumerate(basis):
        M = sum(sp[i]["m"] for i in P) + sum(sp[i]["m"] for i in N)
        J2[idx, idx] += M ** 2
        # J_+ on each occupied orbital
        for i in list(P) + list(N):
            mi = sp[i]["m"]
            mj = mi + 1
            # find orbital j' with same orbit and m = mj
            for k in range(N_SP):
                if sp[k]["orbit"] == sp[i]["orbit"] and abs(sp[k]["m"] - mj) < 1e-9:
                    if i in P:
                        new_P = tuple(sorted(set(P) - {i} | {k}))
                        st = (new_P, N)
                    else:
                        new_N = tuple(sorted(set(N) - {i} | {k}))
                        st = (P, new_N)
                    if st in index_of:
                        # J_+ coefficient: sqrt(j(j+1) - m(m+1))
                        j = sp[i]["j"]
                        coef = np.sqrt(j * (j + 1) - mi * (mi + 1))
                        J2[idx, index_of[st]] += coef * 0.5  # for J_- J_+ term
    # This is a simplified version; full J^2 construction is more involved
    # For now, we extract J from the eigenvector by looking up known J patterns
    return csr_matrix(J2)

# ============================================================
# 7. J → M TRANSFORM OF TWO-BODY MATRIX ELEMENTS
# ============================================================
def J_to_M_tbme(spe, tbme_jt):
    """
    Convert J-scheme TBME to M-scheme TBME for all pairs of SP states.
    Returns: dict (i, j, k, l) -> V_mscheme
    """
    V2 = {}
    # Map SP index → (orbit_two_j, m)
    for i in range(N_SP):
        for j in range(N_SP):
            for k in range(N_SP):
                for l in range(N_SP):
                    sp_i, sp_j, sp_k, sp_l = SP[i], SP[j], SP[k], SP[l]
                    M = sp_i["m"] + sp_j["m"]
                    if abs(M - (sp_k["m"] + sp_l["m"])) > 1e-9:
                        continue
                    V = 0.0
                    # Sum over J, T in J-scheme
                    for (a, b, c, d, J2, T2), V_JT in tbme_jt.items():
                        # Map (a,b,c,d) to (two_j values)
                        tj_a, tj_b = a, b
                        tj_c, tj_d = c, d
                        if (tj_a, tj_b) != (sp_i["two_j"], sp_j["two_j"]):
                            continue
                        if (tj_c, tj_d) != (sp_k["two_j"], sp_l["two_j"]):
                            continue
                        cg1 = CG(tj_a, int(2*sp_i["m"]), tj_b, int(2*sp_j["m"]),
                                 J2, int(2*M))
                        cg2 = CG(tj_c, int(2*sp_k["m"]), tj_d, int(2*sp_l["m"]),
                                 J2, int(2*M))
                        V += V_JT * cg1 * cg2
                    if abs(V) > 1e-12:
                        V2[(i, j, k, l)] = V
    return V2

# ============================================================
# 8. MAIN
# ============================================================
def main():

        print(f"{nuc}: M=0 dim = {len(basis)} ✓")

    # Transform TBME to M-scheme
    V2_ms = J_to_M_tbme(spe, tbme_jt)
    print(f"M-scheme TBMEs (nonzero): {len(V2_ms)}")

    # Build SPE-by-orbit dict
    SPE_by_orbit = {o["name"]: o["eps"] for o in ORBITS}

    # Diagonalize each nucleus
    results = {}
    for nuc, n_p, n_n in [("22Mg", 4, 2), ("22Na", 3, 3), ("22Ne", 2, 4)]:
        print(f"\n--- {nuc} ---")
        basis = build_mscheme_basis(n_p, n_n, M_total=0.0)
        H = build_H(basis, SPE_by_orbit, V2_ms)
        # G4: Hermiticity
        herm = abs(H - H.T).max()
        print(f"Hermiticity residual: {herm:.2e}")
        assert herm < 1e-10

        T2 = build_T2(basis)

        evals, evecs = eigsh(H, k=10, which='SA', tol=1e-10)
        results[nuc] = {"dim": len(basis), "states": []}
        for e, psi in zip(evals, evecs.T):
            t2 = float(psi @ (T2 @ psi))
            # T from T2: T(T+1) = t2 → T = (-1 + sqrt(1+4t2))/2
            T = (-1 + np.sqrt(1 + 4*max(t2, 0))) / 2 if t2 > -0.5 else 0
            print(f"  E = {e:+.4f} MeV,  <T2> = {t2:+.4f}  → T ≈ {T:.2f}")
            results[nuc]["states"].append({"E": float(e), "T2": t2, "T": float(T)})

    with open("phase_II_B2c_results.json", "w") as f:
        json.dump(results, f, indent=2)

    print("\nDone.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

4. The Bridge: Talmi–Moshinsky Transformation Brackets
To connect coordinate-space subatomic operators to the shell-model $jj$-coupled basis, the standard tool is the Talmi–Moshinsky transformation. This transformation converts two single-particle harmonic-oscillator states in the laboratory frame into a relative-plus-center-of-mass representation:
$$\vert{}n_1 l_1, n_2 l_2; \Lambda\rangle = \sum_{nl, NL} B_{nl, NL; n_1 l_1, n_2 l_2}^{(Q, \Lambda)} \, \vert{}nl, NL; \Lambda\rangle$$
where $Q = 2n_1 + l_1 + 2n_2 + l_2 = 2n + l + 2N + L$ is the conserved oscillator quantum number.
The bracket coefficients $B^{(Q,\Lambda)}$ depend crucially on the phase convention used for the harmonic-oscillator radial wavefunctions. Different references use different conventions:
•	Condon–Shortley angular phases
•	State-dependent radial phases $(-1)^n$ with $n = (e-l)/2$
•	Different definitions of the relative and center-of-mass coordinates
A phase error in these brackets propagates directly into every subsequent two-body matrix element. Worse, an incorrect phase convention may still produce orthogonal brackets—unitarity alone does not diagnose the error.

$$B_{\text{ref}} = -0.7071067811865475$$
with absolute error $2.22 \times 10^{-16}$—the IEEE 754 binary64 machine epsilon. This is not agreement to "good precision." This is agreement at the fundamental limit of double-precision arithmetic.

2. The Physics of Effective Interactions
2.1 The USDB Hamiltonian Is Not a Bare Interaction
The USDB effective interaction is not the bare nucleon–nucleon (NNNN) force. It is a renormalized effective interaction, fitted to reproduce experimental sdsd-shell spectra. Its matrix elements have absorbed the accumulated effects of:
•	Core polarization: virtual excitations of 1616O core nucleons into the valence space
•	Short-range correlations: high-momentum components of the strong force that are not resolved by the valence-space basis
•	Three-body forces: folded down to effective two-body form
•	Truncation-induced renormalizations: the systematic removal of excluded-shell contributions, encoded into effective valence-space operators
This is not a defect of USDB. It is a necessity. A purely bare interaction, projected onto the sdsd-shell valence space, would not reproduce the observed nuclear spectra. The valence space is too small. Effective interactions are the standard solution to this problem, and USDB is one of the most thoroughly validated examples.
2.2 The Operator–Hamiltonian Consistency Requirement
The subtlety arises when a new operator is introduced on top of an effective Hamiltonian. Suppose the Hamiltonian has been renormalized to valence space via a unitary transformation UU:
Heff=P U Hbare U† PHeff=PUHbareU†P
where PP projects onto the valence space. Then any observable OO must be renormalized by the same transformation:
Oeff=P U Obare U† POeff=PUObareU†P
If this is not done — that is, if the bare operator ObareObare is inserted into an effective Hamiltonian calculation — the resulting matrix elements are not physical.
The reason is straightforward: the effective Hamiltonian and the bare operator live in inconsistent Hilbert spaces. The Hamiltonian has been corrected for missing valence-space physics; the operator has not.
2.3 The Farid Operators Are Bare
The Farid F0F0 and F2F2 operators are defined in coordinate space as two-body operators acting on nucleons:
F0=∑i<jf0(rij) τi⋅τjF0=∑i<jf0(rij)τi⋅τj
F2=∑i<jf2(rij)[3τ3iτ3j−τi⋅τj]F2=∑i<jf2(rij)[3τ3iτ3j−τi⋅τj]
In Phase II-B.4d, these operators were projected onto the sdsd-shell valence space using the phase-locked Talmi–Moshinsky brackets. The resulting two-body matrix elements are bare valence-space matrix elements. They have not been renormalized.
The bb-sensitivity observed in Phase II-B.4e is the direct signature of this missing renormalization.

This is exactly the physics of effective-field-theory operator evolution.

4. The Operator-Renormalization Theorem
The underlying principle can be stated compactly:
A physical operator, when projected onto a truncated model space, must be renormalized in the same way as the Hamiltonian. If the Hamiltonian is effective but the operator is bare, the operator's matrix elements are not physical.
This principle has been known in nuclear structure theory since the foundational work of Bloch and Horowitz (1958), Kuo and Brown (1966), and Okubo (1954) / Lee and Suzuki (1980). It is a formal requirement of any shell-model calculation, not a matter of preference.
The Phase II-B.4e data provide the empirical confirmation of this principle in the Farid programme.

5. Three Renormalization Pathways
There are three standard methods for carrying out operator renormalization in the sdsd-shell.
5.1 Valence-Space In-Medium Similarity Renormalization Group (VS-IMSRG)
The modern standard. Starting from a chiral effective field theory interaction, VS-IMSRG evolves both the Hamiltonian and any operator down to the valence space via a continuous unitary transformation. The evolution is governed by the flow equation:
dH(s)ds=[η(s),H(s)]dsdH(s)=[η(s),H(s)]
where η(s)η(s) is the anti-Hermitian generator and ss is the flow parameter. The same equation is applied to the operator:
dO(s)ds=[η(s),O(s)]dsdO(s)=[η(s),O(s)]
VS-IMSRG is self-consistent, systematically improvable, and reproduces USDB-like results for the Hamiltonian when the same valence space is used. It is the current state-of-the-art for nuclear shell-model calculations.
Requirements for implementation:
•	imsrg++ software (open source, available on GitHub)
•	Chiral EFT interaction (e.g., EM1.8/2.0)
•	Computational resources for the sdsd-shell problem (manageable)
5.2 Okubo-Lee-Suzuki (OLS) Folded-Diagram Method
The classical method. Constructs an effective operator via a unitary transformation UU that maps the full Hilbert space onto the valence space:
Oeff=P U O U† POeff=PUOU†P
The transformation UU is determined by requiring that the effective Hamiltonian reproduce the low-lying eigenvalues of the full problem.
Requirements:
•	Multi-shell HO basis (valence + excluded shells)
•	Computational resources for the multi-shell problem (heavy but feasible for light nuclei)
•	Careful handling of the decoupling condition
5.3 Phenomenological bb-Averaging (Not Recommended)
A naive approach would be to fit the bb-dependence away by choosing a single "best" value and treating the variation as a systematic uncertainty. This is not acceptable, because:
•	It hides the physical effect rather than accounting for it
•	It provides no path to systematic improvement
•	It cannot be justified theoretically
