Abstract
Phase II-B.7 defines the controlled transition from previously calculated bare harmonic-oscillator-space finite-range F0/F2F0/F2 matrix elements to consistently evolved effective nuclear operators. Previous stages established the two-body algebra, finite-range radial kernels, Talmi–Moshinsky transformation, sdsd-shell assembly, exact-isospin coherent recovery, full frozen-core finite-range benchmark matrix elements, oscillator-length sensitivity, and the computational boundary beyond which genuine operator renormalization requires external microscopic nuclear-theory input.
The central transformation required is
Okeff=UOkU†,k=0,2Okeff=UOkU†,k=0,2
where UU must be generated consistently from a specified microscopic nuclear Hamiltonian through a controlled VS-IMSRG/Magnus or equivalent unitary transformation. No phenomenological renormalization coefficient may be introduced merely to force agreement with a desired nuclear or gravitational result.
The stage is divided into four sequential gates — G1→G2→G3→G4G1→G2→G3→G4 — corresponding respectively to external-input validation, consistent operator evolution, covariance/convergence analysis, and renormalized A=22A=22 contraction. Gravity data remain completely excluded throughout.
Keywords: Farid Gravity Law, Operator Renormalization, VS-IMSRG, Magnus Expansion, Induced Many-Body Operators, Anti-Circular Firewall, Weak Equivalence Principle, Nuclear Matrix Elements

1. Introduction: The Methodological Imperative
A foundational principle of the Farid Gravity Law is that gravitational acceleration is an emergent property driven by internal intranuclear entropy gradients:
g⃗macro=−c2∑iwi∇Sigmacro=−c2∑iwi∇Si
To test whether this framework yields observable violations of the Weak Equivalence Principle (WEP) — such as those probed by space-borne missions like MICROSCOPE [1] — one must compute exact nuclear matrix elements without injecting circular empirical data.
Previous stages of the programme established the foundational machinery:
•	Ingestion and checksum-locking of the Brown–Richter USDB Hamiltonian [2]
•	Machine-precision phase-locking of Talmi–Moshinsky transformation brackets [3,4] (∼10−16∼10−16 error)
•	Exact-isospin recovery of the A=22A=22 isobaric triplet (22Mg22Mg, 22Na22Na, 22Ne22Ne) with degenerate 0+,T=10+,T=1 eigenvalues at −59.94076755396−59.94076755396 MeV
•	Coherent F0/F2F0/F2 recovery on the actual USDB eigenvectors, confirming ⟨F0⟩=−29⟨F0⟩=−29 and ⟨F2⟩=(+2,−4,+2)⟨F2⟩=(+2,−4,+2)
However, subsequent robustness scans revealed that bare harmonic-oscillator space evaluations exhibit significant oscillator-length (bb) sensitivity — 30%–40%30%–40% shifts for short-range kernels, decreasing to 12%–21%12%–21% for long-range kernels. This diagnostic proved that bare evaluations cannot be treated as final physical charges, necessitating a strict, multi-phase hardening protocol.
This article establishes the protocol for that hardening.

9. Contingency Protocol
In the event that Gate 1 remains blocked for an extended period (defined as failure to obtain the required external input within the current programme planning horizon), the following contingencies are authorized, in order of scientific preference:
9.1 Contingency A — Minimal OLS Folded-Diagram Renormalization
If imsrg++ or an equivalent VS-IMSRG code cannot be obtained, a minimal Okubo-Lee-Suzuki folded-diagram implementation may be constructed from scratch. This requires:
•	Multi-shell HO basis (sdsd-shell + excluded shells)
•	Bloch–Horowitz perturbative expansion of the vertex
•	Verification against known 2-body and light-nucleus spectra
This contingency preserves operator consistency but requires substantial additional development.
9.2 Contingency B — Bare-Operator Uncertainty-Limited Prediction
The bare finite-range matrix elements from Phase II-B.4d may be published as bare-operator predictions with the full 30–40% uncertainty band from Phase II-B.4e. This is scientifically defensible if and only if:
•	The result is explicitly labelled bare
•	The uncertainty is fully propagated
•	No gravity data influences the central value
•	The limitation is stated in the abstract and conclusion
This contingency allows the programme to produce a quantitative order-of-magnitude test of the Farid framework at bare-operator accuracy.
9.3 Contingency C — Programme Pause
If neither A nor B is feasible, the validated computational machinery may be published as a methods paper, with physical predictions explicitly deferred. This preserves scientific integrity and provides a firm foundation for future work.
9.4 Prohibited Contingency
Under no circumstances may a phenomenological renormalization factor be introduced to force agreement with a desired nuclear or gravitational outcome. This would violate the anti-circular firewall and compromise the entire programme.

15. Conclusion
Phase II-B.7 establishes the firewall between a successful bare nuclear-operator benchmark and a defensible consistently evolved nuclear matrix element.
Its governing sequence is
Input integrity→consistent evolution→convergence→renormalized contraction→only then external gravity testingInput integrity→consistent evolution→convergence→renormalized contraction→only then external gravity testing
No fitted renormalization constant, preferred gravity signal, or retrospective operator modification is permitted to bridge a failed or missing gate.
The two central scientific commitments of this protocol are:
First, the effective Hamiltonian and the effective operators must be derived from the same unitary transformation. Contracting an evolved operator with unrelated phenomenological wavefunctions is a mixed-framework calculation and is not the default production chain.
Second, the result of even a successful B.7 execution is a renormalized nuclear matrix-element candidate, not a physical nuclear charge. Its reliability depends on the Hamiltonian, truncation, and convergence analysis. Any downstream claim must propagate the full theory uncertainty.
Thus the purpose of Phase II-B.7 is not to guarantee a non-zero Farid effect. Its purpose is to ensure that, if the Effective Farid Even-Isospin Pair Framework is eventually tested against equivalence-principle data, the nuclear quantities entering that test have been determined independently of the gravitational result.
Nuclear theory first. Gravity test second. No circular fitting.Nuclear theory first. Gravity test second. No circular fitting.

Abstract
The transition from microscopic ab initio nuclear theory to macroscopic gravitational testing represents one of the most perilous methodological boundaries in theoretical physics. The risk of circularity—whereby empirical gravitational residuals or Weak Equivalence Principle (WEP) limits covertly tune the nuclear operator pipeline—subverts the falsifiability of any emergent gravity model.
This article establishes Phase II-B.8, the terminal readiness-audit protocol of the Effective Farid Even-Isospin Pair Gravity Framework. The protocol is constructed as an unyielding, sequential firewall separating nuclear-operator evolution from gravitational-data analysis. It is partitioned into four mandatory checkpoint gates (E through H): Renormalized Input Verification, Uncertainty Budget Classification, Firewall Enforcement, and Fit Executability. Each checkpoint has explicit pass criteria, a defined failure taxonomy, and a certificate artifact.
Gravity-data fitting remains strictly locked—Ggravity=LOCKEDGgravity=LOCKED—until every checkpoint achieves absolute programmatic and mathematical clearance. The protocol does not predict a non-zero Farid effect. Its sole purpose is to guarantee that any eventual gravitational test is performed against nuclear quantities that were determined independently of the gravitational result.

Abstract
The integrity of any fundamental-physics programme that compares a theoretical prediction against precision experimental data depends on the impossibility of retroactively adjusting the theory to match the data. In clinical trials this problem is solved by pre-registration and blinding. In particle physics it is solved by blind analysis protocols. In the Farid Even-Isospin Pair Gravity Framework, we extend these techniques to nuclear-structure computation by constructing a cryptographically frozen execution package — a machine-readable specification of all gates, certificates, input manifests, and validation rules that must be satisfied before gravitational data may be examined. The resulting package, F02_B7_v1, is now locked. Its bundle SHA-256 hashes form an auditable chain: any future execution can verify that the protocol was frozen before external nuclear-theory input arrived, and before any gravitational residual was consulted. We describe the architecture of the frozen package, the four-gate cascade it enforces, the certificate hierarchy it produces, and the anti-circular firewall it makes computationally enforceable. The package is currently in the state FROZEN_AWAITING_EXTERNAL_INPUT: nothing has been computed, nothing has been fitted, and gravity-data fitting remains strictly locked. The article is a methodological companion to the physics programme and documents a general technique for enforcing scientific integrity in any computational theory that must eventually confront experimental data.

1. Introduction: The Problem of Retroactive Tuning
1.1 The Universal Vulnerability
Every theoretical physics programme that seeks to compare its predictions against precision experimental data faces the same vulnerability: the temptation to adjust the theory after seeing the data.
This vulnerability is not limited to dishonest practitioners. Even the most careful researcher, working with the best intentions, may unconsciously:
•	Choose a Hamiltonian because it produces a preferred numerical outcome
•	Prefer a regulator scale because it reduces a discrepancy with observation
•	Select a model-space truncation because it makes the predicted effect larger or smaller
•	Adjust an operator definition because the bare value was "obviously too big" or "obviously too small"
The vulnerability is structural, not moral. It arises because the boundary between theory construction and empirical comparison is often blurred, and because the incentives of publication and prestige favour positive results over null ones.
1.2 Existing Solutions in Other Disciplines
Other fields have developed robust defences against this vulnerability:
Field	Defence Mechanism
Clinical medicine	Pre-registration, blinding, data monitoring committees
High-energy physics	Blind analysis, hidden signal region, frozen analysis plans
Cosmology	Pre-registered cosmological parameters, blind likelihoods
Genomics	Pre-registered gene sets, held-out validation cohorts
Each of these fields has learned — sometimes through painful experience — that scientific integrity cannot be guaranteed by good intentions alone. It must be enforced by procedure.
1.3 The Farid Programme's Contribution
The Farid Even-Isospin Pair Gravity Framework extends this tradition to nuclear-structure computation. The framework computes nuclear matrix elements M0,22RM0,22R and M2,22RM2,22R that must eventually be compared against Weak-Equivalence-Principle data from experiments such as MICROSCOPE [1]. The risk of retroactive tuning in this context is severe because:
1.	The nuclear matrix elements depend on many theory choices (Hamiltonian, regulator, model space, kernel form, truncation)
2.	The experimental data are extraordinarily precise (∼10−15∼10−15)
3.	The predicted signal, if it exists, is expected to be small
The solution adopted in Phase II-B.7 is a cryptographically frozen execution package — a machine-readable specification of all gates, certificates, and input manifests, sealed with SHA-256 hash chains, that must be satisfied in full before any gravitational data may be examined.

6. What the Frozen Package Does Not Do
It is important to be explicit about the limitations of the frozen package.
6.1 It Does Not Guarantee Physical Correctness
A frozen protocol guarantees procedural integrity, not physical truth. If the underlying Hamiltonian is wrong, or the operator definitions do not correspond to nature, the frozen package will faithfully execute a wrong calculation.
6.2 It Does Not Eliminate Theoretical Uncertainty
The frozen package preserves uncertainty. It does not reduce it. The theoretical uncertainty from regulator dependence, truncation, and Hamiltonian choice is propagated through the certificate chain but not eliminated.
6.3 It Does Not Replace Physics
Pre-registration is a methodological safeguard, not a physical theory. The frozen package is useful only insofar as the underlying physics is well-posed. It cannot rescue a poorly motivated operator or a badly chosen Hamiltonian.
6.4 It Cannot Guarantee Future Compliance
If a future researcher ignores the frozen package and publishes a result outside its constraints, no cryptographic seal can prevent them. The frozen package is a safeguard against honest error and unconscious bias, not against deliberate fraud.

Part 1 — B.7C-1: Mathematical Specification
§1. Second-Quantized Hamiltonian
The most general Hamiltonian in a finite single-particle basis is:
H=E0+∑ijfij ai†aj+14∑ijklΓijkl ai†aj†alak+136∑ijklmnWijklmn ai†aj†ak†anamal+⋯H=E0+ij∑fijai†aj+41ijkl∑Γijklai†aj†alak+361ijklmn∑Wijklmnai†aj†ak†anamal+⋯
with:
•	E0E0 — scalar (vacuum energy)
•	fijfij — one-body (Fock) matrix
•	ΓijklΓijkl — antisymmetrized two-body matrix element
•	WijklmnWijklmn — antisymmetrized three-body matrix element
Truncation (IMSRG(2)): retain operators up to the two-body level.
§2. Reference State and Normal Ordering
Choose a single Slater determinant ∣Φ⟩∣Φ⟩ as reference. Normal-order all operators with respect to ∣Φ⟩∣Φ⟩:
H=⟨Φ∣H∣Φ⟩+∑ijfij:ai†aj:+14∑ijklΓijkl:ai†aj†alak:+⋯H=⟨Φ∣H∣Φ⟩+∑ijfij:ai†aj:+41∑ijklΓijkl:ai†aj†alak:+⋯
Normal ordering ensures:
•	fij=0fij=0 for hole-hole and particle-particle diagonal terms (absorbed into E0E0)
•	E0=⟨Φ∣H∣Φ⟩E0=⟨Φ∣H∣Φ⟩ is the reference energy
§3. IMSRG Flow Equation
Introduce a flow parameter s∈[0,∞)s∈[0,∞) and evolve the Hamiltonian via:
dH(s)ds=[η(s),H(s)]dsdH(s)=[η(s),H(s)]
where η(s)η(s) is an anti-Hermitian generator: η†=−ηη†=−η.
The evolved Hamiltonian remains Hermitian for all ss: H(s)†=H(s)H(s)†=H(s).
§4. The White Generator
The White generator is defined by the off-diagonal part of HH divided by the appropriate energy denominator:
ηij=fijΔijfor off-diagonal (i,j)ηij=Δijfijfor off-diagonal (i,j)
where:
•	fijfij — one-body matrix element
•	Δij=fii−fjjΔij=fii−fjj — difference of diagonal energies (particle-hole) or the appropriate denominator for pp/hh sectors
The generator drives off-diagonal matrix elements to zero.
§5. The Magnus Expansion
The unitary transformation is written as:
U(s)=eΩ(s)U(s)=eΩ(s)
where Ω(s)Ω(s) is anti-Hermitian: Ω†=−ΩΩ†=−Ω.
The flow of ΩΩ is governed by the Magnus expansion:
dΩds=∑n=0∞Bnn! adΩn(η)dsdΩ=n=0∑∞n!BnadΩn(η)
where:
•	BnBn — Bernoulli numbers (B0=1B0=1, B1=−1/2B1=−1/2, B2=1/6B2=1/6, ...)
•	adΩn(η)=[Ω,[Ω,…[Ω⏟n,η]…]]adΩn(η)=[nΩ,[Ω,…[Ω,η]…]]
Truncation (IMSRG(2)): truncate the Magnus expansion at n=2n=2.
§6. Operator Evolution
For any operator OkOk, the effective operator is:
Okeff=eΩ(∞) Ok e−Ω(∞)Okeff=eΩ(∞)Oke−Ω(∞)
Key requirement: The same Ω(∞)Ω(∞) must be used for both HeffHeff and OkeffOkeff to preserve consistency.
§7. Truncation Scheme
In IMSRG(2):
•	HH retains E0E0, ff, ΓΓ only
•	ηη retains foff-diagfoff-diag, Γoff-diagΓoff-diag
•	ΩΩ retains operators up to two-body
•	Three-body and higher induced terms are dropped
The dropped terms constitute the truncation uncertainty, which must be estimated separately.

Part 2 — B.7C-2: Python Validation Harness
§9. Core Module — imsrg_core.py
python
"""
B.7C-2 — Minimal IMSRG validation harness.
Exact-solvable systems only. No production A=22 calculation.
"""

import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp


class IMSRGTwoLevel:
    """
    IMSRG(1) flow for a 2-level system.
    H = [[a, v], [v, d]]  with reference state |0>.
    White generator: eta = v / (a - d)  [anti-Hermitian]
    """

    def __init__(self, a0, d0, v0):
        self.a0, self.d0, self.v0 = a0, d0, v0

    # --- exact reference ---
    def exact_eigenvalues(self):
        H = np.array([[self.a0, self.v0], [self.v0, self.d0]], dtype=float)
        return np.sort(np.linalg.eigvalsh(H))

    # --- flow RHS ---
    def _rhs(self, s, y):
        a, d, v = y
        if abs(a - d) < 1e-14:
            return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]
        eta = v / (a - d)
        da = 2.0 * eta * v
        dd = -2.0 * eta * v
        dv = eta * (d - a)
        return [da, dd, dv]

    # --- flow ---
    def flow(self, s_max=100.0):
        sol = solve_ivp(
            self._rhs, [0.0, s_max], [self.a0, self.d0, self.v0],
            rtol=1e-12, atol=1e-14, dense_output=True, method='RK45'
        )
        a, d, v = sol.y[:, -1]
        return a, d, v

    def evolved_eigenvalues(self):
        a, d, v = self.flow()
        H = np.array([[a, v], [v, d]], dtype=float)
        return np.sort(np.linalg.eigvalsh(H))


class IMSRGOperatorEvolution:
    """
    Operator evolution under the same White generator.
    O_eff = e^Omega O e^{-Omega}
    For 2-level: explicit 2x2 form.
    """

    def __init__(self, a0, d0, v0):
        self.a0, self.d0, self.v0 = a0, d0, v0

    def _rhs_H(self, s, y):
        a, d, v = y
        if abs(a - d) < 1e-14:
            return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]
        eta = v / (a - d)
        return [2 * eta * v, -2 * eta * v, eta * (d - a)]

    def _rhs_Omega(self, s, y_Omega):
        # y_Omega = [omega_01]  (anti-Hermitian: Omega = [[0, omega], [-omega, 0]])
        # For 2-level, Omega flow = eta (White generator, B_0 = 1)
        # Higher-order terms are zero for 2x2 anti-Hermitian matrices
        H_state = self._H_at(s)
        a, d, v = H_state
        if abs(a - d) < 1e-14:
            return [0.0]
        eta = v / (a - d)
        return [eta]

    def _H_at(self, s):
        sol = solve_ivp(
            self._rhs_H, [0.0, s], [self.a0, self.d0, self.v0],
            rtol=1e-12, atol=1e-14, dense_output=True
        )
        return sol.y[:, -1]

    def omega_infinity(self, s_max=100.0):
        sol = solve_ivp(
            self._rhs_Omega, [0.0, s_max], [0.0],
            rtol=1e-12, atol=1e-14, dense_output=True
        )
        return sol.y[0, -1]

    def evolve_operator(self, O, s_max=100.0):
        """Evolve a 2x2 Hermitian operator O."""
        omega = self.omega_infinity(s_max)
        Omega = np.array([[0, omega], [-omega, 0]], dtype=float)
        # Matrix exponential for 2x2 anti-Hermitian
        from scipy.linalg import expm
        U = expm(Omega)
        return U @ O @ U.conj().T
§10. Test Suite — test_two_level.py
python
import numpy as np
from imsrg_core import IMSRGTwoLevel, IMSRGOperatorEvolution

def test_two_level_spectrum():
    """V5 — Exact diagonalization agreement."""
    cases = [
        (0.0, 1.0, 0.5),
        (0.0, 2.0, 1.0),
        (-1.0, 1.0, 0.3),
        (0.0, 5.0, 2.0),
    ]
    print("--- V5: 2-level exact diagonalization ---")
    all_pass = True
    for a0, d0, v0 in cases:
        solver = IMSRGTwoLevel(a0, d0, v0)
        exact = solver.exact_eigenvalues()
        evolved = solver.evolved_eigenvalues()
        err = np.max(np.abs(exact - evolved))
        status = "PASS" if err < 1e-10 else "FAIL"
        if err >= 1e-10:
            all_pass = False
        print(f"  a0={a0}, d0={d0}, v0={v0}: "
              f"exact={exact}, IMSRG={evolved}, err={err:.2e} [{status}]")
    return all_pass


def test_operator_invariance():
    """V3, V4 — Zero and identity operator invariance."""
    print("--- V3/V4: Operator invariance ---")
    a0, d0, v0 = 0.0, 1.0, 0.5
    evolver = IMSRGOperatorEvolution(a0, d0, v0)

    # Zero operator
    O_zero = np.zeros((2, 2))
    O_zero_eff = evolver.evolve_operator(O_zero)
    err_zero = np.max(np.abs(O_zero_eff))

    # Identity operator
    O_id = np.eye(2)
    O_id_eff = evolver.evolve_operator(O_id)
    err_id = np.max(np.abs(O_id_eff - O_id))

    print(f"  Zero operator residual: {err_zero:.2e} "
          f"[{'PASS' if err_zero < 1e-12 else 'FAIL'}]")
    print(f"  Identity operator residual: {err_id:.2e} "
          f"[{'PASS' if err_id < 1e-12 else 'FAIL'}]")

    return err_zero < 1e-12 and err_id < 1e-12


def test_hermiticity_unitarity():
    """V1, V2 — Hermiticity and unitarity of evolution."""
    print("--- V1/V2: Hermiticity and unitarity ---")
    from scipy.linalg import expm
    a0, d0, v0 = 0.0, 1.0, 0.5
    evolver = IMSRGOperatorEvolution(a0, d0, v0)
    omega = evolver.omega_infinity()
    Omega = np.array([[0, omega], [-omega, 0]], dtype=float)
    U = expm(Omega)

    # Unitarity
    U_dag_U = U.conj().T @ U
    err_unitary = np.max(np.abs(U_dag_U - np.eye(2)))

    # Hermiticity of an arbitrary evolved operator
    O = np.array([[0.3, 0.7], [0.7, -0.2]])
    O_eff = U @ O @ U.conj().T
    err_herm = np.max(np.abs(O_eff - O_eff.conj().T))

    print(f"  Unitarity residual: {err_unitary:.2e} "
          f"[{'PASS' if err_unitary < 1e-12 else 'FAIL'}]")
    print(f"  Hermiticity residual: {err_herm:.2e} "
          f"[{'PASS' if err_herm < 1e-12 else 'FAIL'}]")

    return err_unitary < 1e-12 and err_herm < 1e-12


def test_commuting_operator():
    """V7 — Operator commuting with H is invariant."""
    print("--- V7: Commuting-operator invariance ---")
    a0, d0, v0 = 0.0, 1.0, 0.5
    H = np.array([[a0, v0], [v0, d0]])
    # Build an operator commuting with H (e.g., H itself)
    evolver = IMSRGOperatorEvolution(a0, d0, v0)
    H_eff = evolver.evolve_operator(H)
    # H_eff should equal diag(lambda_minus, lambda_plus)
    exact_eigs = np.sort(np.linalg.eigvalsh(H))
    H_eff_eigs = np.sort(np.linalg.eigvalsh(H_eff))
    err = np.max(np.abs(exact_eigs - H_eff_eigs))
    print(f"  Eigenvalue agreement for H itself: {err:.2e} "
          f"[{'PASS' if err < 1e-10 else 'FAIL'}]")
    return err < 1e-10


def run_all():
    print("=" * 60)
    print("B.7C-2 IMSRG Validation Suite")
    print("=" * 60)
    results = {
        "V5": test_two_level_spectrum(),
        "V3_V4": test_operator_invariance(),
        "V1_V2": test_hermiticity_unitarity(),
        "V7": test_commuting_operator(),
    }
    print("=" * 60)
    print("Summary:")
    for key, val in results.items():
        print(f"  {key}: {'PASS' if val else 'FAIL'}")
    print(f"  Overall: {'PASS' if all(results.values()) else 'FAIL'}")
    print("=" * 60)
    return all(results.values())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_all()

In this upgrade, we detail the complete upgraded analytic structure of the IMSRG(2) commutator, correcting previous truncations and providing an unambiguous roadmap for runtime code certification.
2. Second-Quantized Framework and Reference Normal Ordering
2.1 General Operator Decomposition
Working within a finite single-particle basis $\{\phi_i\}$, any arbitrary operator $A$ up to the two-body level is decomposed with respect to a reference Slater determinant $\vert{}\Phi\rangle$: 
$$A = A^{(0)} + A^{(1)} + A^{(2)}$$
where the normal-ordered components read:
•	Zero-Body (Scalar): $A^{(0)} = \langle \Phi \vert{} A \vert{} \Phi \rangle$
•	One-Body: $A^{(1)} = \sum_{ij} A_{ij} \, :a_i^\dagger a_j:_\Phi$
•	Two-Body: $A^{(2)} = \frac{1}{4} \sum_{ijkl} A_{ijkl} \, :a_i^\dagger a_j^\dagger a_l a_k:_\Phi$
with antisymmetrized two-body matrix elements satisfying $A_{ijkl} = -A_{jikl} = -A_{ijlk}$.
2.2 Reference Occupation Geometry
Let the reference occupation numbers be $n_a = \langle \Phi \vert{} a_a^\dagger a_a \vert{} \Phi \rangle \in \{0, 1\}$ and $\bar{n}_a = 1 - n_a$. The reference expectation values incorporate contraction sums over the occupied Fermi sea:
$$E_{\text{ref}} = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{ij} \Gamma_{ijij} \, n_i n_j, \qquad f_{pq} = \sum_{i} \Gamma_{piqi} \, n_i$$
3. Upgraded Analytic IMSRG(2) Commutator Expressions
Let $C = [A, B]$, where both $A$ and $B$ are truncated at the normal-ordered two-body level. Expanding the commutator via generalized Wick's theorem yields components up to rank three:
$$C = C^{(0)} + C^{(1)} + C^{(2)} + C^{(3)} + \cdots$$
3.1 Zero-Body Component ($C^{(0)}$)
The scalar part receives contributions exclusively from purely contracted $[1B, 1B]$ and $[2B, 2B]$ streams:
$$\boxed{ C^{(0)} = \sum_{ab} (n_a - n_b) \, A_{ab} B_{ba} + \frac{1}{4} \sum_{abcd} n_a n_b \bar{n}_c \bar{n}_d \left( A_{abcd} B_{cdab} - B_{abcd} A_{cdab} \right) }$$
3.2 One-Body Component ($C^{(1)}$) — Upgraded Complete Form 
The one-body commutator block receives contributions from three distinct physical contraction topologies: 
$$\boxed{ \begin{aligned} C^{(1)}_{ij} ={}& \sum_a \left( A_{ia} B_{aj} - B_{ia} A_{aj} \right) \\ &+ \sum_{ab} (n_a - n_b) \left( A_{ab} B_{biaj} - B_{ab} A_{biaj} \right) \\ &+ \frac{1}{2} \sum_{abc} \left( n_a n_b \bar{n}_c + \bar{n}_a \bar{n}_b n_c \right) \left( A_{ciab} B_{abcj} - B_{ciab} A_{abcj} \right) \end{aligned} }$$
•	Methodological Note: The final term representing the induced $[2B, 2B] \to 1B$ occupation-weighted contraction is mandatory. Omitting it yields a code that passes basic Hermitian checks but fails exact Fock-space closure.
3.3 Two-Body Component ($C^{(2)}$) — Upgraded Complete Form
The two-body commutator block incorporates mixed $[1B, 2B]$, full antisymmetrized $[2B, 2B]$, and particle-hole recoupling terms:
$$\boxed{ \begin{aligned} C^{(2)}_{ijkl} ={}& \sum_a \Big( A_{ia} B_{ajkl} + A_{ja} B_{iakl} - B_{ijal} A_{ak} - B_{ijka} A_{al} \Big) \\ &- \sum_a \Big( B_{ia} A_{ajkl} + B_{ja} A_{iakl} - A_{ijal} B_{ak} - A_{ijka} B_{al} \Big) \\ &+ \frac{1}{2} \sum_{ab} (\bar{n}_a \bar{n}_b - n_a n_b) \left( A_{ijab} B_{abkl} - B_{ijab} A_{abkl} \right) \\ &+ C^{(2)}_{\text{ph},\,ijkl} \end{aligned} }$$
where $C^{(2)}_{\text{ph}}$ represents the explicit particle-hole recoupling structure governed by index permutation operators $P_{ij}, P_{kl}$:
$$\boxed{ C^{(2)}_{\text{ph}} \propto (1 - P_{ij})(1 - P_{kl}) \sum_{ab} (n_a - n_b) (\cdots) }$$
3.4 Induced Three-Body Component ($C^{(3)}$) 
Consistent with the IMSRG(2) truncation scheme, the induced three-body tensor generated by $[2B, 2B]$ brackets is explicitly isolated: 
$$\boxed{ [2B, 2B] \supset C^{(3)} \neq 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad C \longrightarrow C^{(0)} + C^{(1)} + C^{(2)} }$$
This term is discarded in IMSRG(2), and its Frobenius norm serves as the primary metric for truncation-error estimation.

The In-Medium Similarity Renormalization Group (IMSRG) has become the standard ab initio framework for evolving nuclear Hamiltonians and arbitrary operators to truncated valence spaces. Its IMSRG(2) truncation — retaining operator ranks up to two-body while discarding induced three-body and higher terms — is the dominant source of theoretical uncertainty. Validating the IMSRG(2) algebra against an independent reference is methodologically essential, but the standard validation pattern — comparing an analytic formula against a code implementing the same formula — is vulnerable to shared errors: if the analytic formula is incomplete, both sides agree while both are wrong. This article presents an exact Fock-space coefficient extractor that constructs the reference-normal-ordered commutator [A,B][A,B] directly from the anticommutation algebra in a finite fermionic Fock space, without using any analytic IMSRG commutator formula. The induced three-body term is confirmed non-zero, with Frobenius norm comparable to the one-body and two-body contributions. The commutator anti-symmetry [A,B]=−[B,A][A,B]=−[B,A] is verified exactly. The extractor provides an independent answer key against which any analytic IMSRG(2) formula can be tested — a decisive check that is not vulnerable to shared errors. All gravitational data remain strictly excluded from the operator-algebra pipeline; the anti-circular firewall is preserved.

1. Introduction
1.1 The IMSRG and Its Truncation
The In-Medium Similarity Renormalization Group [1,2] evolves a Hamiltonian and any other operator via a continuous unitary transformation:
dH(s)ds=[η(s),H(s)],dO(s)ds=[η(s),O(s)]dsdH(s)=[η(s),H(s)],dsdO(s)=[η(s),O(s)]
where η(s)η(s) is an anti-Hermitian generator and ss is the flow parameter. The evolution is implemented as a unitary transformation U(s)=eΩ(s)U(s)=eΩ(s) that decouples the reference state from its excitations.
In practice, the IMSRG equations are truncated. IMSRG(2) retains operators of rank zero, one, and two, and discards induced three-body and higher-rank terms:
C=[A,B]→C(0)+C(1)+C(2)C=[A,B]→C(0)+C(1)+C(2)
This truncation is not an algebraic identity. The induced three-body term C(3)C(3) is non-zero for two-body inputs. Its magnitude determines the truncation uncertainty.
1.2 The Validation Problem
Validating the IMSRG(2) commutator algebra against an independent reference is methodologically essential. The standard validation pattern is:
Analytic formula→compareCode outputAnalytic formulacompareCode output
The code is written from the analytic formula; if the formula is correct, the code passes; if the formula is wrong, the code also passes, because the code implements the same wrong formula. The validation is blind to errors in the reference.
This is not a hypothetical concern. An earlier version of the analytic reference for the IMSRG(2) commutator algebra omitted two essential terms:
•	The occupation-weighted induced [2B,2B]→1B[2B,2B]→1B contraction
•	The particle-hole recoupling Cph(2)Cph(2)
A code written from that incomplete reference would have passed Hermiticity checks, antisymmetry checks, and simple eigenvalue checks — while silently computing the wrong commutator.
1.3 The Independent Validation Lane
This article presents an exact Fock-space coefficient extractor that constructs the reference-normal-ordered commutator [A,B][A,B] directly from the anticommutation algebra:
[A,B]exact=AB−BA[A,B]exact=AB−BA
in the explicit Fock-space representation, without using any analytic IMSRG commutator formula. The result is decomposed into rank blocks via projection onto the quasiparticle basis.
The extractor produces an answer key that is independent of any published formula. When imsrg++ or another authoritative source becomes available, its analytic formulas can be compared against this exact reference, term by term, with no possibility of shared errors.
1.4 Scope and Non-Claims
This article presents:
•	The exact Fock-space construction
•	The rank-block projection and coefficient extraction
•	Numerical validation at machine precision
•	A methodology for independent IMSRG(2) algebra validation
This article does not claim:
•	That the analytic IMSRG(2) formula has been validated (it has not been compared yet)
•	That the full IMSRG(2) flow has been implemented
•	That any physical matrix element has been computed
•	That any gravitational prediction has been made
The article is a methodological contribution to independent validation.

4. Rank-Block Decomposition
4.1 The Quasiparticle Basis
The Fock space is decomposed into blocks by quasiparticle number:
F=⨁k=0NspFkF=⨁k=0NspFk
where FkFk is the subspace with kk quasiparticles.
4.2 Operator Rank
An operator OO is said to have rank kk if it connects the reference-vacuum sector to the kk-quasiparticle sector:
•	Rank 0: acts only on the vacuum
•	Rank 1: connects vacuum to one-quasiparticle states
•	Rank 2: connects vacuum to two-quasiparticle states, or one-quasiparticle to one-quasiparticle states
•	Rank 3: connects vacuum to three-quasiparticle states
The quasiparticle decomposition is the natural basis for rank definition.

9. Methodology and Scientific Integrity
9.1 The Two Failure-Then-Repair Cycles
Two failures occurred during development:
1.	B.7C-3a: The initial rank-algebra reconstruction failed due to a mismatch between integer-ordered Fock states and lexicographically ordered orbital-pair basis. The bug was diagnosed and repaired without altering the PASS criterion.
2.	B.7C-3b: The initial validation design used global least-squares projection, which failed to isolate the reference-normal-ordered rank structure. The design was rejected in favour of an exact Wick-identity test.
Both failures were diagnosed and repaired without altering the physics criterion. The diagnostic history is preserved in the certificates.
9.2 What the Extractor Does Not Claim
•	It does not validate the analytic IMSRG(2) formula (that comparison is pending)
•	It does not replace imsrg++ or any established code
•	It does not compute any physical matrix element
•	It does not make any prediction about nuclear structure or gravitational physics
It is a validation tool. Its value lies in what it enables, not in what it proves.
9.3 The Methodological Principle
The extractor embodies a principle that applies beyond the Farid programme:
When validating an analytic formula against a code, an independent exact reference is essential. Otherwise, shared errors in the analytic formula can pass undetected.
This principle is general. It applies to any computational physics programme that relies on complex analytic formulas.

10. Conclusion
This article has presented an exact Fock-space coefficient extractor for reference-normal-ordered operator commutators. The key contributions are:
1.	An explicit Fock-space construction using canonical anticommutation relations and a Slater-determinant reference.
2.	A rank-block decomposition based on quasiparticle operators, with an exact basis of dimension 1+Nsp2+(Nsp2)2+(Nsp3)21+Nsp2+(2Nsp)2+(3Nsp)2.
3.	Exact coefficient extraction for the commutator [A,B]=AB−BA[A,B]=AB−BA, without using any analytic IMSRG formula.
4.	Machine-precision reconstruction of the exact commutator into its rank blocks C(0),C(1),C(2),C(3)C(0),C(1),C(2),C(3) (relative error 6.17×10−156.17×10−15).
5.	Independent confirmation of the induced three-body term for two-body inputs, with Frobenius norm comparable to the one-body and two-body contributions.
6.	Exact verification of commutator anti-symmetry [A,B]=−[B,A][A,B]=−[B,A].
The extractor provides an answer key against which any analytic IMSRG(2) formula can be tested. When imsrg++ or another authoritative source becomes available, the analytic formula can be compared term by term against this exact reference. This comparison is not vulnerable to shared errors: the reference was constructed without any reference to the analytic formula.
The most important safeguard in physics is not a clever equation. It is a procedure that prevents us from fooling ourselves.

1. Introduction: The Shared-Error Vulnerability
1.1 The Standard Validation Pattern
In computational physics, the validation of an analytic formula typically follows the pattern:
Analytic formula→code upNumerical output→compareReferenceAnalytic formulacode upNumerical outputcompareReference
If the numerical output matches the reference, the implementation is declared correct.
1.2 The Shared-Error Failure Mode
The pattern fails when the analytic formula and the reference are not independent. If the reference is itself an analytic formula — or a previously computed value derived from one — and both the code and the reference share the same error, the comparison will pass while both are wrong.
This failure mode is particularly dangerous in computational nuclear physics, where the IMSRG(2) commutator algebra is complex, the conventions vary between sources, and subtle factors of 2, 1221, occupation numbers, and permutation signs can produce silent discrepancies.
1.3 The Resolution: An Independent Answer Key
The Phase II-B.7C programme addresses this vulnerability by constructing an exact Fock-space coefficient extractor [1] that computes the commutator [A,B]=AB−BA[A,B]=AB−BA directly in a finite fermionic Fock space, without using any analytic IMSRG commutator formula. The result is decomposed into rank blocks C(0),C(1),C(2),C(3)C(0),C(1),C(2),C(3) by projection onto the quasiparticle basis.
The extractor produces an answer key that is independent of any published formula. When the analytic formula becomes available from an authoritative source, it can be compared against this answer key. The comparison is not vulnerable to shared errors because the answer key was constructed without reference to the analytic formula.
1.4 The Need for a Frozen Comparison Protocol
Having an answer key is necessary but not sufficient. The comparison itself must be pre-registered to prevent post-hoc adjustment:
•	The tolerance must be fixed before observing results
•	The stages of comparison must be pre-defined
•	The references and random seeds must be frozen
•	Failure classification must be pre-specified
•	No tolerance may be loosened after a failure
This article presents the frozen Δ-comparison methodology for Phase II-B.7C-3c.

13. Methodological Significance Beyond the Farid Programme
The frozen Δ-comparison methodology is not specific to the Farid Even-Isospin Pair Gravity Framework. It applies to any computational physics programme that:
•	Depends on a complex analytic formula
•	Requires validation against an independent reference
•	Faces the risk of shared errors between formula and code
The general technique comprises:
1.	Construct an independent exact reference (e.g., by direct Fock-space computation)
2.	Freeze the comparison metrics and tolerance before executing
3.	Decompose the comparison into a stage-wise ladder to localize errors
4.	Test with multiple references and random seeds to ensure robustness
5.	Classify failures into pre-specified categories before correction
6.	Bump version on every correction and rerun the full frozen suite
This methodology joins the pre-registration and cryptographic-freezing techniques of Phase II-B.7 as a general contribution to methodological transparency in computational physics.
________________________________________
14. Conclusion
This article has presented a frozen Δ-comparison methodology for validating analytic formulas in computational nuclear physics. The methodology combines:
1.	An independent exact answer key constructed from first principles in a finite Fock space
2.	A pre-registered tolerance (10−1010−10) that must not be loosened after a failure
3.	A stage-wise validation ladder that localizes errors to specific operator-rank combinations
4.	Multiple reference states that test the code's handling of occupation-pattern dependence
5.	A frozen random-seed ensemble that prevents cherry-picking of favorable realizations
6.	A pre-specified failure taxonomy that prevents improvised corrections
7.	A certificate interpretation restricted to the narrow claim the test actually supports
The methodology is applied to the IMSRG(2) commutator algebra. When the analytic formula becomes available from an authoritative source, the exact Fock-space extractor of Phase II-B.7C-3c-IND will provide the reference against which the formula is compared, and the frozen protocol of this article will govern the comparison.
The core methodological principle is:
A mismatch may diagnose the implementation; it may not redefine the theory or the validation target.A mismatch may diagnose the implementation; it may not redefine the theory or the validation target.
The most important safeguard in physics is not a clever equation. It is a procedure that prevents us from fooling ourselves.

Source Identity and Provenance in Computational Physics Validation: The B.7C-3c-SRC Freeze Protocol
Prof. Dr. Md. Faridul Islam Chowdhury
MBBS, MS (Neurosurgery)
Neurosurgeon | Neuroscientist | Theoretical Cosmologist
Founder & Director, Tanfarid Vision Research Institute (TVRI), Bogura, Bangladesh
Inventor of the Tanfarid Quantum Thermodynamic Universe (TQTU) and the Farid Gravity Law
Email: dr_faridul@yahoo.com

Abstract
Validating an analytic formula against an independent numerical reference requires more than having the formula in hand. It requires knowing exactly which version of the formula is being validated. In computational physics, packages evolve over years; tagged releases may lag far behind the development branch; and a formula extracted from an outdated release can silently differ from the formula that will actually be used in production. This article formalizes a source-identity freeze protocol for the Phase II-B.7C-3c analytic IMSRG(2) commutator comparison. The protocol requires that any source used for formula extraction be identified by a triple {branch/tag,commit,archive SHA-256}{branch/tag,commit,archive SHA-256}, that the archive bytes be preserved, and that the formula be extracted from a specific, frozen version rather than from "the repository in general." We document the specific case of imsrg++, where the publicly tagged release v0.1 dates from 2018 while the development branch has since accumulated thousands of commits — a gap large enough that the two cannot be considered interchangeable. The protocol joins the frozen tolerance rules, stage-wise ladder, and failure taxonomy of the preceding runbook as part of a general methodological framework for pre-registered validation in computational physics.
Keywords: Source Provenance, Version Identity, Cryptographic Freezing, IMSRG, Reproducible Validation, Pre-Registration, Anti-Circular Firewall

1. Introduction: The Version Drift Problem
1.1 The Scenario
Suppose an analytic formula for the IMSRG(2) commutator algebra is extracted from a published repository. The formula is implemented in code, and the code is compared against an exact answer key. If the comparison passes, the formula is declared validated.
Now suppose that a year later, the same repository publishes a new release with subtle changes to the formula — a sign convention correction, a permutation operator redefinition, an added induced term. The formula extracted from the old release is no longer the formula in current use. The validation certificate, though formally correct, now certifies a formula that is no longer being used.
This is the version drift problem. It is a real and common failure mode in computational physics.
1.2 The Specific Case
The imsrg++ repository [1] illustrates the problem concretely. Its public releases page lists a tagged release v0.1 dated 2018. The development branch (master) has since accumulated several thousand commits. The two are not interchangeable:
•	v0.1 (2018): the initial public release
•	master (2026+): the current development state, with thousands of intervening changes
A formula extracted from v0.1 and a formula extracted from master may agree on the basic IMSRG(2) structure, but differ in convention details. For the purposes of a precision validation, those details matter.
1.3 The Resolution: Source Identity Freeze
The Phase II-B.7C programme adopts a source-identity freeze protocol: before any formula is extracted, the exact source must be identified by a triple
{branch/tag,commit,archive SHA-256}{branch/tag,commit,archive SHA-256}
and the archive bytes must be preserved. Any future claim that the formula is "the one from imsrg++" must be backed by this triple.
________________________________________
2. The Source-Identity Triple
2.1 Branch or Tag
The first component identifies the reference point. Valid values include:
•	A tag (e.g., v0.1, v1.0, release-2024)
•	A branch name (e.g., master, main, develop)
•	A commit hash
If a tag is used, the tag must be resolved to a commit. Branch names alone are insufficient because they move over time.
2.2 Commit
The second component is the full 40-character commit SHA, not an abbreviated form. This uniquely identifies a snapshot of the repository.
commit=abcdef0123456789...commit=abcdef0123456789...
2.3 Archive SHA-256
The third component is the SHA-256 hash of the source archive (typically a .tar.gz or .zip file). This seals the entire archive, including every file, every line, every comment.
archive SHA-256=abcdef...archive SHA-256=abcdef...
2.4 Why All Three Are Necessary
•	Branch/tag alone is insufficient because branches move.
•	Commit alone is insufficient because a malicious actor could push a different commit with the same hash (computationally infeasible in practice, but the archive hash provides defense in depth).
•	Archive SHA-256 alone is insufficient because the same archive could be reconstructed from different sources.
The triple is the minimum viable identity.
________________________________________
3. The Extraction Protocol
3.1 Step 1 — Acquisition
The source archive is acquired from the upstream repository at the specific commit. The acquisition method is recorded:
•	URL
•	Date and time
•	Method (git clone, direct download, mirror)
3.2 Step 2 — Hash Verification
The archive is hashed and the hash recorded. If the upstream repository provides a published hash, it is cross-checked. If not, the hash is the sole reference going forward.
SHA-256(archive)=recordedSHA-256(archive)=recorded
3.3 Step 3 — Formula Extraction
The specific formula is extracted from the archive. The extraction records:
•	File path within the archive
•	Line numbers
•	Exact text as found
•	Any surrounding comments or documentation
3.4 Step 4 — Convention Mapping
If the source uses a different notation than the validation code, the mapping is documented:
•	Index ordering conventions
•	Antisymmetrization conventions
•	Occupation number conventions
•	Normalization factors
3.5 Step 5 — Freeze
After extraction and mapping, the formula is frozen. Any subsequent modification — even a correction — is treated as a new version with a new identity.
________________________________________
4. The Specific imsrg++ Case
4.1 The Release Situation
Aspect	Value
Publicly tagged release	v0.1 (2018)
Master branch commit count	~3,297 (as of the search snapshot)
Time gap	~8 years
Interchangeable?	No
4.2 The Correct Choice
The Phase II-B.7C programme does not use the v0.1 release as the authoritative source. It uses the current development state — but only after the specific commit is identified and the archive hash is recorded.
4.3 What This Means in Practice
The formula extracted from master at commit XX may differ from the formula extracted from v0.1. The Phase II-B.7C validation will compare against whatever formula is actually in the source we freeze. If this formula differs from the code path actually used in production (which may itself be a later commit), the validation is specific to the frozen commit and no further claims are made.
4.4 The Downstream Anchor
The NuHamil-public documentation [3] confirms that generated NN and 3N matrix elements are compatible with imsrg++ input. This establishes that the software architecture is realistic. However, this compatibility statement applies to the general imsrg++ interface, not to a specific commit. The specific commit used for production may need to be re-identified when the time comes.

8. Methodological Generalization
8.1 Beyond the Farid Programme
The source-identity freeze protocol is not specific to imsrg++ or the Farid programme. It applies to any computational physics validation that depends on:
•	An external source package
•	A formula extracted from that package
•	A comparison against an independent reference
The general protocol is:
1.	Identify the exact source version by a triple {branch/tag,commit,archive SHA-256}{branch/tag,commit,archive SHA-256}
2.	Preserve the archive bytes
3.	Extract the formula verbatim
4.	Map conventions to the validation code
5.	Freeze the extracted formula
6.	Compare against the exact answer key under pre-registered tolerance
7.	Document the result with the source triple attached
8.2 Relationship to Pre-Registration
The source-identity protocol is a specific instance of the general principle of pre-registration. Just as the tolerance, the comparison metrics, and the failure taxonomy are frozen before execution, so is the source identity. The result is a validation certificate that can be independently reproduced years later — because the exact source used is known.
8.3 The Broader Principle
A validation certificate without source identity is a certificate for an unnamed formula.
The source-identity freeze ensures that the certificate names the formula it certifies.
________________________________________
9. What the Source-Identity Freeze Does Not Do
•	It does not validate the formula (that is the role of the comparison)
•	It does not establish that the formula is correct (that is the role of the exact answer key)
•	It does not certify the full IMSRG(2) flow, the White generator, or the Magnus integration
•	It does not replace any part of the production code
It is a prerequisite for the comparison, not the comparison itself.
________________________________________
10. Conclusion
This article has formalized a source-identity freeze protocol for validating analytic formulas in computational physics. The protocol requires that any source used for formula extraction be identified by a triple {branch/tag,commit,archive SHA-256}{branch/tag,commit,archive SHA-256}, that the archive bytes be preserved, and that the extracted formula be frozen before comparison.
The imsrg++ case illustrates the need concretely: the publicly tagged release v0.1 dates from 2018, while the development branch has since accumulated thousands of commits. The two cannot be considered interchangeable for precision validation.
The protocol joins the frozen tolerance rules, the stage-wise validation ladder, the occupation-pattern tests, the random-seed ensemble, and the failure taxonomy as part of a general methodological framework for pre-registered validation.
The current status is:
B.7C-3c-SRC=AWAITING SOURCE BYTESB.7C-3c-SRC=AWAITING SOURCE BYTES
No further theoretical work is required to proceed. When the frozen source archive is available, the protocol executes in a single pass: SHA-256 → source routine extraction → convention mapping → frozen multi-seed Δ-test → machine-readable PASS/FAIL certificate.
A validation certificate without source identity is a certificate for an unnamed formula.

1. Introduction: Why a Source-Arrival Protocol Is Needed
1.1 The Bottleneck
The Phase II-B.7C programme has reached a well-defined boundary. The independent exact answer key (B.7C-3c-IND) has been validated. The frozen Δ-comparison methodology (B.7C-3c-RUNBOOK) has been written. The source-identity freeze protocol (B.7C-3c-SRC) has been formalized.
But the analytic comparator — the formula that must be tested against the exact answer key — has not yet been extracted. It requires source bytes from an authoritative code (e.g., imsrg++ at a specific commit).
B.7C-3c-ANA=AWAITING SOURCE BYTESB.7C-3c-ANA=AWAITING SOURCE BYTES
1.2 Why Not Improvise at Arrival
A natural response to this bottleneck would be to wait for the source to arrive and then improvise the comparison. This would be a methodological error. If the comparison is designed at the moment of execution, the risk of post-hoc adjustment is significant:
•	A tolerance might be chosen to match the observed residual
•	A stage might be added or skipped based on intermediate results
•	A failure might be repaired by relaxing the criterion
The Source-Arrival Protocol eliminates this risk by freezing the entire comparison plan in advance. At source arrival, there are no decisions to make — only steps to execute.
1.3 Scope
This article specifies:
•	The source-identity triple and acquisition procedure
•	The formula extraction and convention mapping
•	The frozen comparison metrics and tolerance
•	The stage-wise validation ladder
•	The occupation-pattern and random-seed tests
•	The failure taxonomy
•	The certificate issuance rule
It does not specify the analytic formula itself. The formula is what the source provides.
________________________________________
2. The Source-Identity Triple
2.1 Required Components
Before any formula is extracted, the source must be identified by:
{branch/tag,commit,archive SHA-256}{branch/tag,commit,archive SHA-256}
•	Branch or tag: reference point in the repository history
•	Commit: full 40-character commit SHA
•	Archive SHA-256: cryptographic hash of the source archive
2.2 Prohibited Substitutions
•	A branch name without a resolved commit is insufficient (branches move)
•	An abbreviated commit SHA is insufficient (must be full 40 characters)
•	An archive from a mirror without upstream hash cross-check is insufficient
2.3 Specific Note on imsrg++
The publicly tagged release v0.1 (2018) is not interchangeable with the current master branch. The master branch has accumulated thousands of intervening commits. The protocol uses whatever commit is explicitly frozen — not "the repository in general."
2.4 Identity Record
The source identity is recorded in the format specified in Appendix A. The record is attached to the final certificate.
________________________________________
3. Acquisition and Verification
3.1 Acquisition
The source archive is obtained by a documented method:
•	git clone at the specific commit
•	Direct download of an archive from the upstream releases page
•	Download from an authorized mirror with hash cross-check
The acquisition records:
•	URL
•	Date and time (ISO 8601)
•	Method
•	Operator identity (if applicable)
3.2 Hash Verification
SHA-256(archive)=recorded and comparedSHA-256(archive)=recorded and compared
If the upstream provides a published hash, it is cross-checked. If not, the computed hash becomes the sole reference.
3.3 Preservation
The archive is preserved without modification. Any future re-verification uses the preserved archive, not a fresh download.

4.1 Targeted Extraction
Only the specific routines needed for the IMSRG(2) commutator comparison are extracted. The extraction records:

•	Line numbers
•	Exact text as found
•	Any surrounding comments or documentation

Antisymmetrization	...	...	...
Occupation numbers	...	...	...

4.3 Freeze
After extraction and mapping, the formula is frozen. Any subsequent modification — even a correction — is treated as a new version requiring a new source-identity triple and a full rerun.

10. Failure Classification
If a failure occurs, it is classified into exactly one of the following categories before any correction is attempted:
Category	Description
INDEX_CONVENTION_ERROR	Index ordering mismatch
PERMUTATION_SIGN_ERROR	Wrong sign in permutation operator
NORMALIZATION_FACTOR_ERROR	Factor of 2, 1221, or similar

OCCUPATION_FACTOR_ERROR	Wrong nana or nˉanˉa weighting

ANTISYMMETRIZATION_ERROR	Two-body tensor not correctly antisymmetrized
SOURCE_TRANSCRIPTION_ERROR	Mismatch between source and code
EXACT_EXTRACTOR_REGRESSION	The answer key itself has changed
UNRESOLVED_ALGEBRA_MISMATCH	Cause not yet diagnosed
10.1 Correction Rule
A correction is permitted only when it follows independently from the frozen source/convention. No correction may be chosen merely because it reduces ΔΔ.
10.2 Version Bump
After any correction, the implementation receives a new version identifier and the complete frozen test suite is rerun.

14. Methodological Generalization
The Source-Arrival Protocol is a specific instance of a general technique in computational physics:
When a validation depends on an external source, the entire comparison plan should be frozen before source arrival.
The general protocol comprises:
1.	Identify the source by a triple {branch/tag,commit,archive SHA-256}{branch/tag,commit,archive SHA-256}
2.	Preserve the archive bytes
3.	Extract the formula verbatim
4.	Map conventions
5.	Freeze the comparison metrics, tolerance, stage ladder, references, and seeds
6.	Execute without modification when source arrives
7.	Classify failures into pre-specified categories
8.	Bump version on any correction
This technique applies to any computational physics programme that validates an external source against an independent reference.

Abstract
The IMSRG(2) commutator algebra underlies every operator-evolution calculation in the In-Medium Similarity Renormalization Group, from effective Hamiltonians to transition operators to hypothetical new-physics couplings. Its validation has, until now, relied on agreement between analytic formulas and codes implementing those same formulas — a methodology vulnerable to shared errors. This article reports a decisive validation. Using authoritative published uncoupled commutator equations (Stroberg et al., Phys. Rev. C 110, 044316 (2024), Appendix A, Eqs. A3–A5), we compare the analytic IMSRG(2) zero-body, one-body, and two-body components against an independently constructed exact Fock-space answer key. The initial runtime failed with Δ2max⁡=18.9651Δ2max=18.9651, diagnosed as a SOURCE_TRANSCRIPTION_ERROR: the AA/BB two-body tensors in the negative terms of the [1B,2B][1B,2B] contribution were interchanged in the local code. The bug was corrected from the published expression — no tolerance, seed, reference, or physics criterion was altered. The frozen validation suite (3 references × 5 seeds = 15 cases) was rerun in full. Maximum discrepancies: Δ0=8.15×10−15Δ0=8.15×10−15, Δ1=2.33×10−13Δ1=2.33×10−13, Δ2=1.96×10−13Δ2=1.96×10−13. The frozen threshold of 10−1010−10 was comfortably satisfied. The exact Fock-space reconstruction residual was 5.63×10−135.63×10−13. This establishes a machine-precision bridge between published analytic IMSRG(2) commutator conventions and an independent exact answer key, closing the Phase II-B.7C-3c validation ladder. All gravitational data remain excluded; the anti-circular firewall is preserved.
Keywords: IMSRG(2) Commutator Algebra, Exact Fock-Space Answer Key, Source-Transcription Error, Published Analytic Convention, Machine-Precision Agreement, Anti-Circular Firewall

1. Introduction
1.1 What This Validation Achieves
The In-Medium Similarity Renormalization Group (IMSRG) is the standard ab initio framework for evolving nuclear Hamiltonians and arbitrary operators to truncated valence spaces [1,2]. Its IMSRG(2) truncation — retaining operator ranks up to two-body while discarding induced three-body and higher terms — is the dominant source of theoretical uncertainty.
Validating the IMSRG(2) algebra against an independent reference is methodologically essential. The standard validation pattern — comparing an analytic formula against a code implementing the same formula — is vulnerable to shared errors. If the analytic formula is incomplete and the code is written from the same incomplete formula, both sides agree while both are wrong.
This article reports the resolution of that vulnerability for the IMSRG(2) commutator algebra.
1.2 The Two Lanes
The validation compares two independent constructions:
Lane A — The Exact Fock-Space Answer Key. The commutator [A,B]=AB−BA[A,B]=AB−BA is computed directly in a finite fermionic Fock space, without using any analytic IMSRG commutator formula. The result is decomposed into rank blocks C(0),C(1),C(2),C(3)C(0),C(1),C(2),C(3) by projection onto the quasiparticle basis [3].
Lane B — The Published Analytic Convention. The uncoupled IMSRG(2) commutator equations from Stroberg et al. [4], Appendix A, Eqs. A3–A5, are implemented in code, with the permutation convention explicitly defined by the paper.
The comparison is term-by-term at each operator rank.
1.3 Scope and Non-Claims
This article reports a specific validation result. It does not claim:
•	That the full IMSRG(2) flow has been validated
•	That the generator, the Magnus expansion, or the flow ODE has been validated
•	That the current imsrg++ source code matches the published equations line by line
•	That any physical matrix element has been computed
•	That any gravitational prediction has been made
The validation is restricted to the algebraic commutator structure at the 0B0B, 1B1B, and 2B2B levels.
________________________________________
2. The Published Analytic Equations
2.1 Source
The authoritative reference is:
Stroberg, S. R., et al., Phys. Rev. C 110, 044316 (2024), Appendix A, Eqs. A3–A5.
The paper provides uncoupled commutator equations for reference-normal-ordered one- and two-body operators, with the permutation convention explicitly specified. These equations form the analytic comparator (Lane B).
2.2 Convention
Two-body matrix elements are antisymmetrized:
Apqrs=−Aqprs=−Apqsr=AqpsrApqrs=−Aqprs=−Apqsr=Aqpsr
Reference-state occupation numbers satisfy np∈{0,1}np∈{0,1} and nˉp=1−npnˉp=1−np.
Permutation operators PijPij, PklPkl are simple index exchanges, without an implicit sign.
2.3 The Three Rank Components
The commutator C=[A,B]C=[A,B] is decomposed into:
•	C(0)C(0) — zero-body (scalar)
•	Cpq(1)Cpq(1) — one-body
•	Cpqrs(2)Cpqrs(2) — two-body
For two-body inputs, the exact commutator also contains a rank-33 component C(3)C(3), which IMSRG(2) discards by truncation prescription.
________________________________________
3. The Exact Fock-Space Answer Key
3.1 Construction
The exact answer key [3] is constructed in a finite Fock space with Nsp=6Nsp=6 single-particle modes (26=6426=64 states). The commutator is computed by direct matrix multiplication:
Cexact=AB−BACexact=AB−BA
without any analytic formula.
3.2 Rank Decomposition
The exact operator is decomposed into its rank blocks via projection onto the quasiparticle basis:
Cexact=Cexact(0)+Cexact(1)+Cexact(2)+Cexact(3)Cexact=Cexact(0)+Cexact(1)+Cexact(2)+Cexact(3)
The reconstruction error at machine precision confirms the completeness of the decomposition.
________________________________________
4. The Initial Failure and Its Diagnosis
4.1 The First Runtime
The initial implementation of the published equations produced:
Δ2max⁡=18.9651Δ2max=18.9651
This is a large, unambiguous failure. The frozen tolerance of 10−1010−10 was exceeded by nine orders of magnitude.
4.2 Stage-Wise Diagnosis
Rather than adjusting the formula to fit the observed result, the stage-wise validation ladder was applied:
Stage	Result
[1B,1B]→0B+1B[1B,1B]→0B+1B	✅ PASS
[2B,2B]→0B+1B+2B[2B,2B]→0B+1B+2B	✅ PASS
[1B,2B]→1B+2B[1B,2B]→1B+2B	❌ FAIL
[2B,1B]→1B+2B[2B,1B]→1B+2B	❌ FAIL
The failure was localized to the mixed [1B,2B][1B,2B] and [2B,1B][2B,1B] contributions. The diagonal and pure-two-body terms were correct.
4.3 Root Cause: SOURCE_TRANSCRIPTION_ERROR
A careful comparison of the local code against the published expression (Eq. A5 of the source paper) revealed that the AA and BB two-body tensors were interchanged in the negative terms of the [1B,2B][1B,2B] contribution.
This is a pure transcription error: the published formula is correct, but the local code transcribed it incorrectly.
4.4 The Correction
The correction was made from the published expression only. No tolerance, seed, reference, or physics criterion was altered.
This is the critical methodological point. The failure was not repaired by fitting to the exact answer key. It was repaired by reading the published formula correctly.

When Sir Isaac Newton published his universal law of gravitation in 1687, he established a mathematical masterclass in celestial mechanics while leaving the ontological source of mass entirely unexamined. For over three centuries, physics treated mass as an axiomatic charge. In 2010, Erik Verlinde attempted to pierce this black box by proposing that gravity is an entropic force emerging from holographic information density on boundary screens. While Verlinde's proposal offered an imaginative exit from the anomalies of dark matter and spacetime curvature, it remained an abstract thermodynamic assumption, leaving the microscopic "bricks" of the entropic house completely undefined and struggling against stringent MOND and solar-system constraints. This article presents a rigorous comparative and foundational treatise on the Farid Gravity Principle. We demonstrate that macroscopic gravity ($g = -c^2 \nabla S$) does not originate from arbitrary thermodynamic information bits or macroscopic holographic assumptions. Instead, it arises natively from the Proton–Neutron Microscopic Matrix—an explicit subatomic decomposition of quark, gluon, sea, binding, and relativistic spin energies into weighted gravitational sources. Through a four-stage derivation culminating in the recovery of Newton’s Poisson equation ($\nabla^2 \phi = 4\pi G \rho$), we show how universal nucleon spin absorbs into a redefinition of $G$, while internal coherence constraints are strictly bounded by MICROSCOPE mission limits ($\eta_{AB} < 10^{-15}$). All dark matter and dark energy placeholders are discarded; gravity is revealed as the macroscopic echo of confined subatomic spin and motion.

1. Introduction: Newton’s Unopened Box and Verlinde’s Thermodynamic Leap
When Sir Isaac Newton formulated his inverse-square law of gravitation, he provided an extraordinarily successful description of how massive bodies interact across space. Yet, Newton was acutely aware of an underlying philosophical and physical gap. Writing "hypotheses non fingo" ("I feign no hypotheses"), he acknowledged that his equations could calculate how gravity acts, but not what physical property of matter causes it to act. Confined by the 17th-century horizon of science, atomic structure, subatomic particles, intrinsic spin, and mass-energy equivalence were entirely unknown. Newton was forced to treat mass ($\rho$) as an unexamined primitive axiom.
For over three hundred years, physics accepted mass as a fundamental charge of nature without asking what microscopic machinery generates it.
In 2010, string theorist Erik Verlinde published a groundbreaking paper proposing that gravity is an emergent entropic force caused by changes in the information associated with the positions of material bodies. Verlinde derived Newton’s law of gravity from classical statistical mechanics by applying the holographic principle—assuming a closed spherical boundary surface with $N$ bits of binary information encoded on a holographic screen, related to energy via the equipartition rule and $E = mc^2$. Later, in 2016, Verlinde argued that his approach would modify Newtonian laws to explain galaxy rotation curves without dark matter, mirroring Milgrom’s Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND).
The Critical Flaw in Verlinde’s Approach
While Verlinde’s work was praised for originality, it suffered from a fatal structural deficit: he tried to build an entropic house starting from the roof (the macroscopic holographic screen) without knowing what the bricks were made of.
•	The Empty Source: Verlinde could never answer where information and entropy fundamentally originate. He assumed the presence of space, boundaries, and degrees of freedom as primitives.
•	Phenomenological Limitations: As Milgrom, Sanders, Famaey, and McGaugh pointed out, Verlinde’s emergent gravity formula is of limited applicability, failing to reproduce rich MOND phenomenology in disk galaxies, internal multi-body dynamics, or solar-system constraints without arbitrary tuning of acceleration scale constants ($a_0$).
The Farid Gravity Principle breaks through this barrier by discarding magical placeholders like dark matter, dark energy, and curved empty spacetime, opening the exact black box that Verlinde could not enter.
2. The Proton–Neutron Microscopic Matrix: The True Physical Origin
The Farid framework does not rely on open-ended thermodynamic assumptions or abstract boundary screens. It originates entirely from the Proton–Neutron Microscopic Matrix—an explicit decomposition of subatomic internal dynamics.
Instead of viewing mass as an unexplained primary charge, the Farid Principle establishes the ontological chain:
$$\boxed{\text{Microscopic subatomic dynamics} \longrightarrow \text{Effective source functional} \longrightarrow \text{Macroscopic gravitational field}}$$
Stage I: The Nucleon-Level Scalar Functional
To bridge subatomic mechanics and macroscopic fields without falling into vector cancellation traps (where random spin orientations cancel out so $\sum \mathbf{S}_i \approx 0$), we operate strictly on scalar magnitudes at the nucleon scale ($N$ = proton or neutron):
$$\boxed{ q_F^{(N)} = \frac{\hbar}{2 c L_{\text{coh}}} + \lambda_C \mathcal{C}_N }$$
1.	The Universal Spin Term ($\frac{\hbar}{2 c L_{\text{coh}}}$): Represents the absolute scalar magnitude of the nucleon’s intrinsic angular momentum. It is strictly positive, ensuring that the source does not vanish even when spins are randomly oriented. The characteristic macroscopic length scale, $L_{\text{coh}}$, converts angular momentum into an effective mass-equivalent scale.
2.	The Collective Coherence Term ($\lambda_C \mathcal{C}_N$): Accounts for the influence of the surrounding quantum environment. The parameter $\mathcal{C}_N$ ($0 \le \mathcal{C} \le 1$) denotes microscopic coherence, a dimensionless state variable depending on temperature, pressure, and nuclear structure.
Methodological Safeguard: Binding energies and internal kinetic energies are strictly excluded from this functional because they are already fully accounted for in the standard mass-energy tensor ($E_{\text{known}}/c^2$). To include them would constitute a fatal double-counting error.
3. Aggregation, Coarse-Graining, and Field Collapse
Stage II: Atomic Aggregation
Transitioning to a neutral atom containing $Z$ protons, $N$ neutrons, and $Z$ electrons via linear additivity:
$$\boxed{ Q_F^{(A)} = \sum_{p=1}^{Z} q_F^{(p)} + \sum_{n=1}^{N} q_F^{(n)} + \sum_{e=1}^{Z} q_F^{(e)} }$$
•	Nucleon Dominance: Protons and neutrons comprise over $99.9\%$ of the atomic source.
•	Electron Negligibility: The electron contribution is suppressed by $\approx 1/1836$ relative to nucleon mass, rendering it negligible for macroscopic sourcing despite identical spin ($\hbar/2$).
Stage III: Macroscopic Coarse-Graining
Performing a coarse-graining integral over a bulk body composed of $N$ nucleons ($M = N m_N$), we derive the effective Farid source density:
$$\boxed{ \rho_F = \frac{\rho}{m_N} \left( \frac{\hbar}{2 c L_{\text{coh}}} + \lambda_C \mathcal{C}_{\text{body}} \right) }$$
Total gravitational source density is thus:
$$\boxed{ \rho_G = \rho + \rho_F }$$
Stage IV: The Inevitable Collapse to Newton’s Poisson Equation
Substituting $\rho_G$ into the generalized Poisson equation yields:
$$\boxed{ \nabla^2 \phi = 4\pi G \rho \left[ 1 + \frac{\hbar}{2 c L_{\text{coh}} m_N} + \frac{\lambda_C \mathcal{C}_{\text{body}}}{m_N} \right] }$$
Through two rigorous collapse mechanisms, material-dependent deviations vanish:
•	Mechanism A (Universal Spin Absorption): Let $\epsilon_S = \frac{\hbar}{2 c L_{\text{coh}} m_N}$. Because this is universal and composition-independent, it is mathematically absorbed into a redefinition of the gravitational constant:
$$G_{\text{eff}} = G (1 + \epsilon_S) \quad \implies \quad \nabla^2 \phi = 4\pi G_{\text{eff}} \rho$$
•	Mechanism B (Coherence Elimination by Experiment): Ultra-precision equivalence-principle tests—most notably the MICROSCOPE mission—constrain differential acceleration to $\eta_{AB} < 10^{-15}$. This forces $\lambda_C \mathcal{C}_{\text{body}} / m_N \equiv 0$ for ordinary matter.
The bracket collapses cleanly to unity:
$$\boxed{ \nabla^2 \phi = 4\pi G \rho }$$

1. Introduction: Disentangling the Two Truncations of Many-Body Flow
1.1 The IMSRG Flow Architecture
The In-Medium Similarity Renormalization Group (IMSRG) provides a systematically improvable framework for decoupling reference states and evolving operators via a continuous unitary transformation parameterized by a flow parameter s:
dsdH(s)=[η(s),H(s)],dsdO(s)=[η(s),O(s)]
where η(s) is an anti-Hermitian generator. Formally, this evolution is equivalent to an explicit similarity transformation:
H(s)=U(s)H(0)U†(s),U(s)=eΩ(s)
where Ω(s) represents the anti-Hermitian Magnus operator governing the unitary path.
1.2 The Dual-Truncation Fallacy
In constructing practical computational engines, developers frequently conflate two completely independent approximations:
1.	Operator-Rank Truncation: Within IMSRG(2), operators are restricted to zero-, one-, and two-body ranks. Induced three-body and higher-rank tensor components generated during commutations are explicitly discarded.
2.	Magnus–Bernoulli Series Truncation: The generator Ω(s) obeys the exact differential equation:
dsdΩ=k=0∑∞k!BkadΩk(η)
where Bk are the Bernoulli numbers and adΩk(η)=[Ω,adΩk−1(η)] denotes the k-fold nested commutator. This series is infinite and requires numerical termination based on a pre-registered convergence threshold.
A critical failure mode in many-body codebases is the unverified assumption that dsdΩ=η (the leading-order shortcut). While this holds exactly when [Ω,η]=0 (such as in diagonal, scalar, or trivial 2×2 systems), it introduces systematic, hidden errors in general non-commuting physical flows.
1.3 Methodological Scope
This article establishes a rigorous matrix-space verification of the full Bernoulli expansion under genuine non-commuting conditions. It does not claim to validate many-body truncation limits or macroscopic nuclear observables; its sole purpose is to prove that the Magnus integration machinery functions with absolute mathematical fidelity.
2. Mathematical Formulation of the Magnus Expansion
2.1 The Bernoulli-Weighted Differential Equation
The exact evolution of the Magnus operator is governed by the Bernoulli expansion:
dsdΩ=k=0∑∞k!BkadΩk(η)
where B0=1, B1=−21, B2=61, B4=−301, and all odd Bernoulli numbers Bk=0 for k≥3.
2.2 Runtime Noncommutativity Detection
To prevent false-positive validations, the system enforces a runtime check:
max∥[Ω,η]∥>0⟹full Bernoulli expansion required
When this inequality is satisfied, truncation at k=0 is mathematically inadmissible.
3. Validation Design and Implementation Harness
3.1 Test Matrix Configuration
A 3×3 Hermitian Hamiltonian H(0) is initialized with non-degenerate diagonal elements and non-zero off-diagonal couplings vij. The anti-Hermitian White generator ηij(s)=ΔijHij(s) drives the decoupling.
3.2 Dual-Route Integration Protocol
•	Route 1 (Direct Flow): Integrates dsdH=[η(s),H(s)] via high-precision adaptive ODE solvers (RK45).
•	Route 2 (Magnus Reconstruction): Integrates dsdΩ via the full Bernoulli series, then constructs HMagnus(s)=eΩ(s)H(0)e−Ω(s) using matrix exponentiation.
Agreement between these independent computational pathways provides an unassailable cross-check of the underlying calculus.

Abstract
The In-Medium Similarity Renormalization Group at the two-body level—IMSRG(2)—is defined by the continuous projection of flow equations onto the normal-ordered zero-, one-, and two-body operator subspace. A prevailing intuition suggests that for a two-fermion system ($A = 2$) in a restricted single-particle basis, physical three-body clusters are absent from asymptotic states, implying that an IMSRG(2) implementation should naturally recover exact results. This article demonstrates that such an assumption is mathematically unfounded. Published IMSRG analyses establish that for a single-determinant in-medium reference, normal-ordered $n$-body (NOnB) truncation guarantees exactness only when $n \ge 2A$. Consequently, for $A = 2$ under an IMSRG(2) framework ($n = 2$), the sufficient exactness condition ($2 \ge 4$) is unsatisfied. A previously documented benchmark failure in Phase II-B.7C-3e ($\Delta E \approx 1.97 \times 10^{-5}$, spectrum drift $3.15 \times 10^{-2}$) must therefore be re-interpreted not as a coding defect, but as genuine IMSRG(2) truncation divergence. To resolve this ambiguity, we formulate the Step-Wise Contraction Bookkeeping Map (B.7C-3e-F1). This protocol decomposes the continuous flow derivative into its $[1B, 1B]$, $[1B, 2B]$, $[2B, 1B]$, and $[2B, 2B]$ rank-producing channels, providing explicit analytical residuals for every zero-, one-, and two-body block alongside the tracked induced three-body norm $N_3(s)$. The core diagnostic relies on an instantaneous mismatch test at $s = 0$: if all retained blocks match to machine precision initially but diverge along the flow trajectory, the discrepancy is classified as EXPECTED TRUNCATION DIVERGENCE. Conversely, initial discrepancies indicate an IMPLEMENTATION/REPRESENTATION MISMATCH. All gravitational data remain strictly excluded; the anti-circular firewall is preserved.
